speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (for Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-10, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have a chance to speak on this important piece of legislation which will implement the budget measures which increase the excise taxes and duties on tobacco products.
All members of the House are aware of the vital link between deficit reduction and economic recovery, and there is no question that these changes in tobacco taxation will have a very beneficial effect on our efforts to get Canada's public finances under control. I want to stress the fact that the reason for making these changes was not essentially to raise taxes or to generate more revenues; it was because of the fact that each year some
35,000	Canadians die as a result of tobacco related illness.
This is an issue that should be of concern to every Canadian. The tax measures themselves will raise additional revenues of $1.4 billion in the 1991-92 fiscal year, declining progressively to $980 million by 1994-95. It is clear that in the language of dollars and cents this initiative makes good sense, but I believe the case for this bill is made in a far more eloquent way when we look at its likely effects on the health of Canadians.
One thing that became abundantly clear to me in my two years as Minister of National Health and Welfare is the inexorable link between tax policy and the reduction of tobacco use. The facts speak for themselves: we brought forward a significant increase in tobacco taxation in the 1989 budget. We combined this action with extensive health promotion programs, a law to end tobacco promotion and regulations requiring health messages on tobacco packages. It was a potent recipe for success.
The result was that in 1989 we saw an incredible 8 per cent drop in per capita tobacco consumption, the largest in history. It is a question of some pride for Canadians that over the last two years, successively, this country has led the world in reducing the use of tobacco. The effect of this is that it will help us to bring down our medical costs in Canada. More important, it will help us dramatically in terms of keeping alive thousands of Canadians who would otherwise have been lost to cruel diseases caused by tobacco.
In terms of taxation, the formula is very simple: when cigarettes are less affordable they are less attractive, especially to our children. Based on previous tobacco consumption trends and estimated deaths from tobacco use, it is likely that this bill will save up to 125,000 young people from becoming hooked on tobacco, meaning at least 35,000 fewer deaths among this age group alone.
If the numbers are hard to understand, imagine an airline passenger jet crashing every second day, or to put it another way, imagine the entire population of a city the size of Cornwall being wiped out each and every year. If these deaths were taking place in that way there would be headline news, not just around Canada but around the world. Because of the nature of the deaths caused by tobacco, it tends to be something that is private, not seen by everybody, personal and individual, the silent mortality that takes place year after year, the tragic waste of human lives, the immense human suffering, both for those who are afflicted by the disease itself and for the survivors who have to manage without their loved ones, often go unnoticed by the rest of us.

Government Orders
It is time that we as a people and as a society begin taking stock of the tremendous cost that tobacco use inflicts upon our population. It is particularly important to those of us who believe that the most important thing we can do for our children is to give them a society in which their health comes first. It is surely time for us today to take this measure to do what we can to reduce tobacco use and to help to save lives in Canada.
To return to the financial realm, consider that each year diseases caused by smoking, such as cancer and heart disease, cost our health care system untold billions of dollars, to say nothing of the lost productivity and the incredible heartache for the families involved.
Let us take a few minutes to look at the mechanics of the legislation. The bill provides for an increase in the excise tax on cigarettes by 3 cents a cigarette, or $6 a carton, as well as a proportionate increase in the excise levies on other tobacco products. This means that the excise tax on manufactured tobacco, which includes loose, fine cut tobacco, will increase by $4.08 per 200 gram container. The ad valorem excise tax on cigars will be raised from 40 to 65 per cent. These tax increases were effective on February 27, 1991.
The bill also addresses concerns about the unequal tax burden on loose tobacco for traditional roll-your-own cigarettes and preportioned tobacco sticks. Prior to the budget, tobacco sticks were taxed as a fine cut product on the basis of weight. However, because tobacco sticks generally weigh less than roll-your-own cigarettes, they were generally less heavily taxed on a per cigarette basis.
Tobacco sticks will now be taxed on a per unit basis, and the excise tax and duty will equalize those on other fine cut products at approximately two-thirds of the rate on fully manufactured cigarettes. Since the excise levies on tobacco products are imposed at the manufacturers' level, the higher tax rates announced in the budget would apply only to tobacco products sold by manufacturers after February 26.
To ensure that the tax increases are applied in a consistent manner at different trade levels, the excise tax increases proposed in the budget will apply to wholesalers' and retailers' inventories held at the time the new rates took effect. To simplify compliance for small and
medium sized retailers, the tax will not apply to the first
1,000	cartons of cigarettes or the equivalent volume of tobacco products held in inventory in retail outlets on budget day.
Consistent with the treatment of remittances of income taxes, this bill also imposes interest on any delay in payment of the increases in excise taxes and duties on tobacco products beyond the time within which existing levies are normally remitted, as well as on late or deficient instalments of the tax on tobacco inventories. Imposing interest on delayed payments will ensure that taxpayers voluntarily remit the tax increases announced in the budget, and that those who withhold payment until the tax increases are enacted are treated equally.
This bill is an important part of the government's plan to ensure that Canada's economy is soundly run, but as I mentioned, it is an even more important element of our strategy to reduce the consumption of tobacco in Canada. In both areas, we have a chance to do an enormous amount of good in ensuring the health and prosperity of our children.
By bringing our nation's finances under control, we can ensure that our children have access to the same programs and prosperity that most of us have enjoyed throughout our lives. By ensuring that our children are Canada's first smoke-free generation, we will bequeath them a far healthier society than the one which we inherited. In this latter field, I believe that we have made encouraging progress. It is clear, however, that much work remains to be done. This bill, with its measures to make tobacco less affordable for our children, is an important step in that direction.
Let me simply conclude by saying to the House that in whatever time any of us have to serve as members of Parliament in this institution, the most important contribution we can make to our country is to take measures which markedly improve the health and the longevity of our citizenry.
This is an opportunity for all members of Parliament to speak with one voice to help ensure that Canadians live healthier and longer lives. This is an opportunity that each of us has, on either side of this House, to do what we can to promote the health of our children. It is an opportunity to reduce human suffering.

I believe that if this House speaks unanimously and strongly today in support of this legislation, we will be making an important contribution not just for this generation but for generations yet to come in Canada.

Madam Speaker, hon. colleagues and government members, thank you for the opportunity to rise today on debate of Bill C-10, an act to amend the Excise Thx Act and the Excise Act.
This bill promotes a tax which by some is called a "sin tax." Others label Bill C-10 a "tax grab." As the Liberal critic for national health and welfare, I see this bill from a different angle. For me it is a bill with the potential to become a health tax. More than that, it has the potential to be the bill to show that this government truly cares about Canadians.
Money from this bill should go to health promotion, education of the dangers of tobacco addiction, aid to tobacco farmers and workers in the tobacco industry and to medicare, to provide the best care possible for people struck down by smoking related illnesses.
If the government would allow this bill to become a health tax, as the minister who has just spoken would like it to be, then Bill C-10 would be a further sign of promise in the fight against disease due to smoking.
This year alone, because of higher tobacco taxes,
700,000	Canadians are expected to quit tobacco. That is over 200,000 people who will be saved from death. One-third of that 700,000 would have eventually died from diseases related to smoking addiction.
In the first quarter of this year, Statistics Canada reported an all-time low in tobacco sales with a drop of
12.2	per cent. These statisticians believe the figure may drop because of people who quit short term for only one or two weeks because of the increase in the price of cigarettes.
What happens to these people? Surely they are more than a statistic. They are people who want to be free of tobacco but cannot break the chains. Why? It is much more than a question of will-power. Addiction to tobacco is one of the strongest addictions known, comparable to alcohol and heroin addictions. We are all acquainted with someone who is trying to quit or who has quit. The ordeal is a painful, arduous journey back from the control of nicotine. Sometimes it takes many attempts before someone is finally able to free himself or herself from the grip of tobacco.
Smokers face three barriers. There is the nicotine
Government Orders
addiction, a physiological craving for it. There are habits and lifestyles such as smoking after a meal or with friends on coffee breaks. There is an emotional reaction which can be as strong as the grief for a lost loved one. We realize that.
Some people try to break the ties but they are unable. These people need more help. They need to learn the nature of the enemy, how to best combat the addiction. Acupuncture, laser therapy, cold turkey and hypnosis; are these the ways people are trying to deal with this addiction? This is a medical problem and it needs medical support and education resources.
Most of Canada's 6.4 million smokers hate the higher taxes, seeing themselves as targets in a make-money revenue scheme. Why? Be reminded that the government has raised taxes 32 times since it came to office in 1984. Others view tobacco taxes as an assault on their rights and freedoms. Nothing is ever that simple. Nonsmoking advocates are not lifestyle police, they are simply people who care for the health of themselves and others. They do not wish ill to the men and women who work in the tobacco industry, but there are some facts which cannot be denied about the nature of the tobacco companies.
They target children. They flaunt government laws and they have blatant disregard for the serious health risks posed by tobacco addiction.
I truly believe that if they were interested in the well-being of their workers they would put some of their money and profits toward retraining in other skills.
Interestingly enough, the president of the Tobacco Manufacturer's Council, a close personal friend of the Prime Minister, will never admit smoking causes disease. In a letter to the former finance minister he commented on the "alleged risks of smoking". I would like to underscore the word "alleged", the alleged risks of smoking. In Canada each year 35,000 smokers die. This is not some happenstance coincidence. This is not an alleged risk. This is a real risk. These people die from diseases caused by their addiction.

Government Orders
Death is never pretty, we all know, especially death due to smoking. The tar and chemicals of decades destroy lung tissue, leaving it blackened and cancerous. Emphysema chokes off the smoker's air, leaving him gasping for life's breath. Only heart disease sometimes strikes quickly. At other times it merely cripples, with the patient living in fear of that paralysing pain shooting through the left side of the chest.
Non-smokers are not immune to smoking diseases. Second hand smoke is also a killer, causing an estimated
53,000	deaths in the United States each year. In Canada, with a smaller population, it is roughly one-tenth the American figure; five thousand Canadians.
Smoking harms the innocent; family members and co-workers. Even the unborn cradled in the womb of the mother can be harmed as chemicals pass from her bloodstream to the developing child.
You must never forget the children. They could be your children or they could be mine, lured to tobacco because of the look, the feel and the cachet of a cigarette. Maybe they are drawn to tobacco because their parents smoke or because all their friends do. Perhaps they are the dupes of the tobacco industry's advertising campaigns, which display smoking as glamorous and cool, the adult thing to do.
Maybe these boys and girls never planned to become smokers with a pack a day demand on their lungs, but it happens. That is the nature of addiction. It pulls youth in and it takes their lives away from them.
In this country a half million children are addicted to tobacco. Because of higher taxes, this year alone 100,000 of these youths are expected to quit. Another 30,000 will never begin, dissuaded by the cost of tobacco.
Your kids and mine could be the smokers of tomorrow unless we move to stop them.
This bill is inherently flawed in its follow through. It is a deterrent to smoking but it offers no help for the people who are most affected by it.
I believe in higher taxes as a deterrent to smoking, as has been shown by a study by the Addiction Research Foundation of Toronto, the health promotion branch of the Ontario Ministry of Health and the tobacco products
section of Health and Welfare Canada entitled "Effects of Pricing On Cigarette Use among Teenagers and Adults in Canada, 1980-1989", released February 1991.
I do not believe in taxing people on the back of an addiction and then leaving them with nothing. This tax should not be another GST. The government calls this tax "part of a comprehensive strategy for reducing tobacco consumption in Canada".
Then why does the government not go the extra mile and put the tax money back into helping the people? Is this a tax grab disguised as health policy? I have here a description of the bill given to me by the office of the Minister of State for Finance. In the second last paragraph on the last line it says: "As well these taxation measures reinforce the government's comprehensive strategy for reducing tobacco consumption in Canada". This seems suspiciously like an afterthought.
Revenues from Bill C-10 should go toward four causes or programs if this government truly is sincere in helping smokers quit and not letting this be a tax grab. First, health promotion and education to give people the facts about smoking. A recent poll showed that the dangers of smoking have not yet registered with the majority of the smokers. The word must get out. People must be informed.
Second, support programs to help people quit. Tobacco addiction is one of the strongest known. To quit requires the help of many people, family and friends, plus health care professionals. Today the resources are simply not there.
Recently I received a report from the Canadian Nurses' Association, released in October 1990. Canadian nurses across the country tell us they need help. They need help with their programs to help nursing students and to help nurses quit smoking. We should support this.
Third, we should establish special funds for medicare. It is cruel for the government to take the tax money of a smoker and not offer him or her any help to break free from nicotine. It seems that the government wants these people to stay addicted, perhaps to line the coffers with tax revenues. Money should also be given back to the medicare system to provide the people and equipment to save as many smokers as possible.

Fourth, there is another group drastically affected by the decrease in smoking, the tobacco farmers. As demand for tobacco decreases, what will happen to these men and women? They need programs to find alternative crops. Diversification will be a necessity in the years to come.
It is my understanding that two programs were established to help tobacco farmers. The Tobacco Transition Adjustment Initiatives program or the TTAI was meant to ease farmers out of the tobacco market. It was meant to retire quota, buying it from farmers and writing it off the books, truly a worth-while initiative.
It was established in 1986, but funding did not start until 1987. In March of next year what is left of the program will die. Ontario, with over 1200 tobacco farmers, will lease the TTAI in March, while New Brunswick lost it in 1989. Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Quebec, which together have fewer than 150 farmers, have had the program extended until March of next year.
This is a program which had a budget of $53.2 million. From C-10 alone the government will earn $1,400 million in one year. I would like to call to the attention of Canadians that this government must be called to task whether this is really a health tax and not a tax grab.
The other program, called the Alternative Enterprise Initiative program, was opened to tobacco farmers to help search for alternative crops. Tobacco grows on a light, sandy soil which few other crops can tolerate, I am told by one report from Agriculture Canada, but there is hope another commercially viable alternative can be found. That is where the research component of the AEI comes into play. Years of research brought canola to Canadian fields. More research might bring help to tobacco farmers.
How much is the government spending on this type of research, development and study? Only $15 million, of which, according to sources at Agriculture Canada, only $10 to $11 million has been allocated. Meanwhile, the government will make $4 billion this year in tobacco taxes alone.
There is one more thing we should know. The government is cancelling the AEI program at the end of this fiscal year.
Government Orders
What are the government plans for the future of this business? Can a "comprehensive strategy" include aid to tobacco farmers?
In March tobacco growers met with the former finance and agriculture ministers to ask for support. To renew TTAI and the tobacco component of the AEI would be one way the government could show its support and true genuine sincerity to the cause.
I have been told by the office of the Minister of State for Finance that together the changes in the excise levies on tobacco products and the new tax on tobacco inventories will raise an additional $1.4 billion in the 1991-92 fiscal year. In the following three years $1.14 billion, $1.03 billion and $980 million will be raised respectively. As I said, this year alone the government will realize $4 billion from taxes and tobacco.
Surely, some money from these billions can go toward helping those saddled with addiction, for education of everyone in every aspect of society, and tobacco farmers. The government must show sincerity and earmark this money for those in need. There is no doubt that taxes on tobacco bring in big money for the government-thousands of millions of dollars. It is also clear that, by the law of diminishing returns, as tobacco taxes increase more people will quit smoking until the revenues realized by these taxes will be diminished.
So what? An estimated $7 billion per year is spent to heal people suffering from diseases related to smoking. There is no possible way to measure the value of these lives to society and to their loved ones. These are real people, not cash cows ready to be milked because of an addiction. There are others already taking advantage of these people: the cigarette companies. These companies target children in their campaigns while arguing they are trying to convince people to change brands. That simply does not compute. Roughly 10,000 Canadians per month light a cigarette for the first time. Most of these people are under the age of 18.
If the companies did not attract kids to smoking they would have no customers, hence no industry. All the smokers will eventually quit. The tobacco industry needs new blood to fuel its business, but unfortunately its business is not what Canadians want at this time. We should help them search for other types of business.

Business of the House
Only then can we truly have a comprehensive strategy against smoking.
With C-10 the gap between the cost of tobacco sticks and loose tobacco is closing. This could break the market for tobacco sticks, indeed. I believe Canadians should have every right to protest taxes, but they must not use this protest in a way that would jeopardize the antismoking campaign to save the lives of our youth. The government should not put profits before people. The government, if it truly cared about Canadians, would take the opportunity of this debate to prove itself an ally of the people of Canada, all of them. There is no excuse.
I ask the government to take necessary action. I also urge the government to help the people of this country be free from tobacco. Educate everyone, warn everyone. Do not be confused by the industry's smoke-screen. Take revenues from C-10 and use them to break the cycle of addiction. Help farmers find alternative crops. Do not settle for half measures if you are truly interested in saving Canadians.
I will end by reading from a story in The Ottawa Citizen that appeared last week, entitled Heavy Smoker-My Father by Janice Kennedy, and I quote:
My father's last four months were spent inside the hospital. He was too weak to get out of bed. And besides, most of the time he was hooked up to some kind of apparatus. The final month he couldn't even speak, having undergone a tracheotomy that eased his painful breathing a little but silenced him.
His final days were marked by a strange, wild-eyed look. It came over him as the plastic breathing tube filled and he fought in desperate silence for air.
The bill before us, if it is truly to be a health tax, must be earmarked for people who would like to stop smoking, for people who are ill as a consequence of smoking. We should also help the industry to find alternative business. In this way we can all be true Canadians concerned for the health and livelihood of all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there have been some discussions to approve the following motion.
That, not withstanding the Standing Orders and usual practices of the House, on Friday June 14, 1991:
In "Routine Proceedings" a government bill placed on notice on Thursday June 13, 1991 be introduced and read a first time and
deemed printed, such bill to be in respect to British Columbia grain handling operations; and
No later than 12.30 p.m., the Minister of Labour shall move second reading of the said bill; and
No later than 1.30 p.m., the Speaker shall interrupt any proceedings then underway and put forthwith and successively without further amendment or debate, all questions necessary to dispose of the said bill at all stages, provided that any request for recorded or deferred divisions on any of the said questions not be receivable; and
That the regular Friday order of business then be called; and
That if the normal hour of daily adjournment is reached and a message from the Senate has not yet been received respecting Royal Assent, the House will suspend to the call of the Chair until such message is to be received; and
That upon returning from such Royal Assent, the Speaker shall forthwith adjourn the House until 11 a.m. on Monday June 16, 1991.

Madam Speaker, we have a problem with the very restrictive House Order that has been presented to the House, for a number of reasons.
First of all, the wording of the House Order as it is presently does not guarantee that any member of the New Democratic Party will have a chance to say anything or ask any questions of the minister. Therefore, before we can agree to this House Order we have to ensure that we have an opportunity to participate, that our positions are stated and that the questions we wish to ask of the minister are asked.
Second, and this is just as important to us, our labour critic has a number of questions that she wants answered by the minister before we can agree to a House order.
We want to ensure we know what we are entering into and what the minister's intentions are before we agree to something which in effect prevents any chance by the opposition to really delay the government's intentions.
We want to know exactly what the minister is up to, what he is going to guarantee to the workers and their families in this situation before we agree to any particular House order.

Madam Speaker, my colleague has indicated our concerns about this legislation. I have three questions that I would like to ask the minister for a clear response before we proceed with this motion.

The first question is will the minister assure the workers in the Grain Workers' Union and their families that he will not accept an arbitrated 12-hour award, which would be in contravention of other legislation, unless the two parties have agreed to the 12-hour award?
Second, will he, if the arbitrator suggests it, agree to an independent commission to look at the impact of the 12 hours on workers' health and safety and on their families? Would that commission be made up of something like a lawyer, a doctor and one other? In addition, would he agree to work with me to improve legislation in the federal jurisdiction in the future to try to avoid some of these kinds of situations?
Third, would he agree not to proclaim part two pre-emptively prior to there being a dispute in Prince Rupert?

Madam Speaker, with regard to the three questions asked by the labour critic for the NDP concerning the continuous hours of work and the 12-hour shifts, the Canada Labour Code prohibits such a practice now unless both parties agree.
If they agreed, through a voluntary collective agreement, to such a system of work then most likely I would also agree. My interpretation would be this. If a 12-hour work shift, 12 continuous hours of work, was imposed by an arbitrator in a collective agreement, then to me that would not have been voluntary agreement by the workers. In that particular case, it would still be contrary to the Labour Code and in that case, of course, I would not breach the Labour Code.
The second point is that the hon. member asks whether I would be agreeable to an industrial inquiry if asked for by the mediator arbitrator. I would like to remind my hon. friend that I gave instructions to my top officials about this issue when they went to Vancouver earlier this week to meet with the parties. When Mr. McDermott met with the unions, this idea of an industrial inquiry was well received by the unions. It was not well received by management.
Business of the House
Of course, if asked by the mediator-arbitrator to proceed on that route, I would certainly be very agreeable to facilitate that.
With regard to her third question, whether I would agree to work with her with a view to improving industrial relations in the federal sector in Canada, I would certainly be willing to do that. At the same time, I would remind her that Labour Canada has definitely the best record of any provincial jurisdiction in its settlement of collective agreements as we do settle over 90 per cent of them without work stoppages. But that does not mean that there is not room for improvement. Of course, I would be very happy to work with her to study that matter and see how we can improve our industrial relations contracts in Canada.
With regard to her last question, how we would proclaim Part II of the proposed legislation, I can give my word to my hon. friend that there will be no proclamation of that, until and if, there was a work stoppage. Even then, there will be no proclamation until there was consultation with my friends from the opposition.

Madam Speaker, I rise to resume debate on Bill C-10.1 find myself in the strange position of being in full support of the government on this piece of legislation.
I think legislation that increases the tax on tobacco, if it is viewed properly as a health measure rather than as a revenue measure, is to be applauded. Of course, the bill will increase the tax by about $6 a carton, or 3 cents a cigarette. It will raise approximately $1.4 billion this year, reducing down to $980 million in three years. It will raise $1.4 billion in the first year.
It is interesting, of course, that the Minister of Communications and the former minister of health spoke on this bill. I think he should be congratulated because when he was the minister of health he brought forward a number of anti-smoking initiatives that have paid off for Canadians.
One of the things we have learned in relation to cigarette smoking is that there is a correlation between the tax rate and the number of people who smoke. An increase in cigarette taxes will immediately reduce consumption by 8 per cent to 12 per cent. It has been
estimated that if cigarette taxes are increased 20 per cent, it would reduce the total number of smokers by
800,000	if you added together those people who would quit smoking and those who would not start smoking.
Since the government has initiated a combination of accelerating tax increases and anti-smoking campaigns, including bans on advertising in 1984, there has been to the end of 1990 a decline of 40 per cent in Canada of smokers. This is one of the better records in the industrial world.
It is important that we put into perspective what the implications are for Canadian society of the use of tobacco. Tobacco-related illnesses now kill 38,000 people in Canada a year, 38,000 Canadians. It kills more Canadians than alcohol, drug abuse, car accidents, industrial accidents, fires, murder, suicide and AIDS combined. So it is by far one of the major causes of death in Canada.
In addition, it costs untold billions of dollars within our health care system to treat people who have smoke-related illnesses. At a time when our community is trying to grapple with the increase in our health care costs, and trying to develop efficiencies and ways of reducing expenditures, there is probably no more positive step that the government can take to reduce health expenditures, than to reduce the consumption rate of tobacco.
I do want to spend a little bit of time talking about the reactions from the tobacco companies. The tobacco companies, led by that friend of the government's Bill Neville, have started a mail-back campaign to try to convince the government that it should reduce the tax on tobacco products.
This mail-back campaign is in clear violation of the Tobacco Control Act. I still feel that the federal government should have immediately initiated court action seeking an injunction to prohibit this mail-back campaign pending the decision of the Quebec court as to the legality or the charter worthiness of that piece of legislation.
It is interesting that the tobacco companies had maintained that one of the reasons they were opposing the Tobacco Control Act is that they did not have the technical capability to put inserts in tobacco products with health warnings on. They did not have the ability to do that by the deadline of June 1, and therefore were delaying it.

At the same time, how hypocritical they were when they, all of a sudden, decided that they would have a mail-back campaign. They had the immediate technology to print and put inserts into tobacco packages to direct a message to the Prime Minister.
It is this kind of hypocrisy from the tobacco industry that is so characteristic of its approach. It is very important that Canadians fully realize what the tobacco companies have been doing in relation to promotion of their products.
Documents filed before the Quebec Superior Court indicate very clearly, I will use the words of the member for North York, insidious, pernicious and unethical tactics used by the tobacco industry advertisers to sell death to youths and to other healthy consumers.
The documents filed in that court very clearly spell out what the tobacco industry and the health community already know. To get people to smoke, one must get them early. Ninety per cent of all smokers start before they are 18. A study was done in the United Kingdom that clearly documented this. Ninety per cent of all smokers started before they were 19.
I guess I have something to relate to that. I started smoking when I was 13 or 14, and I smoked for far too many years, up to my early thirties, two or three packs a day. I know the kind of image that the tobacco industry portrayed. It was geared to young smokers, and that was one of the reasons I got involved in smoking. This is repeated time and time again.
The tobacco industry, from the confidential memos that were obtained in a court in Quebec, clearly indicated that they were targeting those as young as 12 years old. Some of the things that were revealed in the court case were that when numerous studies were linking smoking to death by cancer and heart attacks, tobacco companies were still conducting extensive research on young smokers.
It clearly showed that that industry is dominated by companies which respond most effectively to the needs of young smokers. What the tobacco companies found is that if they are going to survive, they have to cater to young smokers. Studies in England showed that they have to recruit 300 new smokers a day to replace the ones who are dying off at the other end. This is what the companies do. They realize that the youth is their major target group. Documents before that court stated very
Government Orders
clearly: "Young smokers represent the major opportunity group for the cigarette industry. We should therefore determine their attitudes to smoking and health and how this might change over time."
It goes on to say that they realize serious efforts to learn to smoke occur between the ages of 12 and 13 in most cases. It also says that they have been able to document among users that starters no longer believe the dangers of smoking and they universally assume that the risks do not apply to themselves.
This is one of the characteristics of young people. When one talks about all types of hazards, they have a tendency to assume a sense of bravado, of risk taking. They think that risks apply to somebody else, whether that is driving a car fast, taking risks in outdoor adventures or starting smoking. They like to take risks, so they simply say: "Those risks don't apply to us and we are willing to take that risk if it gains us something".
One of the things that the tobacco industry discovered in its research was that very young starting smokers choose Export A because it provides them with an instant badge of masculinity, appeals to their rebellious nature and establishes their position among their peers. In other words, the tobacco industry did research on the dynamics of teenagers and adolescents and then developed a product that would appeal to that rebellion, to their masculinity and to their acceptance among their peers, all of which are very, very important to teenagers.
The tobacco industry is certainly, at this point in time, desperately trying to protect its share of the market and its profits. It is initiating the mail-back campaign, not because of any concern about taxes in Canada, but because it is frightened that the government's efforts to reduce cigarette smoking are being successful. Those government efforts are based on a double-barrelled approach of raising taxes and prohibiting a type of advertising.
One of the things on which I think the government has not been aggressive enough is in the matter of tobacco advertising. It has brought in some legislation under the Tobacco Control Act, but it has not rigorously pursued the enforcement of that. It has not taken the initiative and proclaimed the regulations that were supposed to be in place on June 1. It has not stopped the tobacco mail-back campaign and it has not proceeded with other recommendations.

The health committee has looked at this issue and people have said repeatedly that there should be a total ban on all tobacco advertising, including a ban on promotion. One of the things that the companies like to do very much is say: "We are not advertising, we are promoting a sports event, or a cultural event". But, of course, their brand names, their company logos, all of the things, their colours that are identified with their brands and with cigarette smoking, are used to promote their product.
New Zealand did a major study of 33 countries, looking at the impact of the banning of tobacco advertising. They found conclusively that the banning of tobacco advertising does have a dramatic impact on the number of smokers and the recruitment of new smokers.
I want to turn my attention now to what I think the government should be doing in relation to the revenues which it has-

Madam Speaker, the North American High School Organization network is a Jewish student movement with representation across Canada. The issue of Syrian Jewry is of great concern to them.
At present there is an urgent call for action against the Syrian government due to the torturous acts and oppressive conditions which Syria is inflicting upon the Jews living there. These Jews are not allowed to emigrate; they are often beaten, tormented, abducted and imprisoned. They are denied the basic human rights, according to the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights to which Syria is a signatory.
An example of this is the case of Elie and Selim Swed. They were imprisoned for three and a half years without
being charged and were constantly tortured. They were recently sentenced to six and a half more years in prison in a trial where they were not allowed a lawyer or to speak, and no charges were made public.
The Government of Canada has always supported the cause of oppressed Jewry and human rights. Along with all members of this House, I call upon the government of Syria to comply with the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights and allow those Syrian Jews who wish to emigrate to do so freely.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on this date in 1841, 150 years ago, the first Parliament of the United Canadas opened in Kingston, Ontario. The opening of Parliament marked the reunion of Upper and Lower Canada in one province and established the ground work for Confederation some 26 years later.
Though the new Parliament started slowly with newspapers of the day referring to it as the "do nothing but talk session", spumed on by the development plans of Governor General Sydenham, it eventually passed acts which provided for the purchase of and expansion of the Welland Canal, for improving navigation aids in the St. Lawrence River, and for building new roads. In addition, a new Board of Works was established to oversee ambitious new construction projects.
Madam Speaker, as Canadians debate the future of our country, let us remember the work of our ancestors 150 years ago. They knew then what we must remember today, that our future prosperity lies in a united Canada, not in a nation divided.

Madam Speaker, having had an opportunity recently to visit the People's Republic of China, I rise today to encourage the Government of Canada to move toward normalization of trade relations with China.

Northern Telecom, Ingersoll-Rand Canada, Alcan and Lamko Tool & Mold are examples of recent successful joint ventures in China.
My recent visit demonstrated to me that more trade with China would in fact be helping the people of China raise their standard of living, not to mention that it would create jobs in Canada also.
The policy of reform and opening to the outside world should be encouraged as it is the road to lead China to economic and social prosperity.
Japan, Italy, Australia, Britain and the United States have taken steps to normalize relations with China. I encourage Canada to do the same.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to denounce one aspect of a recently issued report by a group of former politicians and industrialists who refer to themselves as Group 22. This group calls on the federal government to completely withdraw from the national health care system. The report states that the federal government should have no role to play in health care and that existing federal involvement, namely maintenance of national standards and banning of extra billing and user fees, should disappear.
We know that the Prime Minister was personally briefed by members of this group and it is reported that he was "genuinely interested" and "impressed" with the report. Canadians would like to know exactly which recommendations the Prime Minister is interested in and impressed with.
Madam Speaker, on March 29 this year the government voted against a Liberal motion stating "that this House reaffirms its commitment to medicare". The recent comments by the Prime Minister reinforce his government's lack of commitment not only to medicare but also to the well-being of all Canadians.
I urge the Prime Minister and his government to disregard this aspect of the report and maintain national health care standards under the Canada Health Act and more, restore adequate funding for Canada's medicare, the envy of the world.

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the Eritrean People's Liberation Front in its call for a free, fair and open referendum on the future of Eritrea.
Forty years ago, the great powers forced an unhappy Eritrea to join with its traditional enemy, Ethiopia. The ensuing war caused between 250,000 and 350,000 deaths in Eritrea alone.
Now the war is apparently over, but long-term stability is far from guaranteed. Sectarian fighting continues, and millions of people are still dying of starvation and avoidable disease in the Horn of Africa. A secure lifeline of assistance to these people is possible only if Ethiopia's wasteful and destructive civil war comes to a permanent end.

More specifically, obtaining a permanent solution to the problems of this region will require a peaceful settlement of the status of Eritrea that respects the wishes of the majority of the Eritrean people.

I therefore urge the Canadian government to follow the example of Sweden, Denmark, Norway and other countries in upholding the right of the Eritrean people to define their own future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was both amazed and disappointed when I heard the Reform Party's narrow-minded and outmoded views on multiculturalism.
The party's statements merely help spread misconceptions about our policy in this area. Multiculturalism is based on the concept that all Canadians have the same economic, political and social rights. It is a concept that favours equality and is opposed to racism and discrimination.
The Reform Party and its leader are urging Canadians to believe in myths that can only breed discord. At a time when Canadians are trying to strengthen their unity, multiculturalism remains one of the most powerful tools this country has ever had to achieve that goal.

I would like to repeat, for the benefit of members of the Reform Party, that this government is intent on using every means at its disposal to help create a Canadian identity that everyone of us can truly share.

Madam Speaker, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is about to impose another disastrous policy on Atlantic fishermen, user pay dockside monitoring.
The government had two alternatives. It could have retained the past system of hailing, log books and random checks. This would have meant a bit of work for fishery officers. It could have gone to a system which the industry wanted called the "paper chase" because of so much paperwork for the fishermen and the processors to keep accurate records for the Department of Fisheries, because it does not trust anyone.
What did the fishermen get? They got the weigh master system, an employment program sponsored by the Department of Fisheries which the department wanted and which will mean longer waits and much higher fees to the fishermen who have to foot the bill.
No one supports this new system, as has been seen in Newfoundland, and will be seen in Nova Scotia and other areas.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has once again ignored the fishermen and gone ahead with a policy that has no benefit for those involved.

Madam Speaker, after reading Marjorie Nichols column in the June 13 Citizen, I was gratified to think that there is at least one member of the media who is willing to take the time to research its articles and to print the true facts instead of distorted untruths.
Is it any wonder that we hear so much negativism from Canadians across this country when they are exposed to a steady diet of gloom and doom, distortions and misinformation.
The media must start taking its role in society seriously and start acting in a non-partisan, responsible way, giving Canadians the facts and nothing but the facts, and
letting them make up their own minds as to the effectiveness of this government's policies.

Madam Speaker, the spirit of multiculturalism is ultimately the spirit of Canadian unity. Multiculturalism makes it possible for all Canadians to fully contribute to the building of a stronger and more united Canada.
The Canadian Multiculturalism Act unanimously adopted by the Parliament of Canada seeks to remove the barriers that divide us from one another, barriers such as racism and discrimination.
In its repeated attacks on multiculturalism the Reform Party and its leader shows it knows little or nothing of what this great countiy is all about.
On the other hand in the Globe/CBC poll in April 84 per cent of Canadians, 84 per cent said any new constitutional arrangement must reflect the multicultural nature of Canada. It is very easy to appeal to people's fears and uncertainties. It is very difficult to build a society of fairness and equality of opportunity for all. Mr. Manning has chosen the easy path. This government, which has done so much to bring a new vision to Canada, will not.

Madam Speaker, I have raised the issue of Montreal and its dramatic economic situation in the House many times. We have had a debate in this House on the situation in Montreal, and the people of Montreal are becoming increasingly concerned. Recently, the Quebec Caucus, which I have the honour to chair, discussed the sad fact of a declining economy, increasing poverty and lack of employment in the Montreal region. I had the privilege of seconding the motion in which the leader of our party, Jean Chretien, took an active part. And now we have the minister responsible for Montreal, the hon. member for Anjou-Riviere-des-Prairies and Minister of Transport, again saying sorry, he is not responsible and the economy in general is to blame, this at a time when jobs at Air Canada and at the Bank of Canada's branch for foreign exchange services are being moved to Toronto. Once again, the minister has not been doing his job.
June 14, 1991

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry but the hon. member's time has expired. The hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap.

Madam Speaker, up to one third of Quebec's bookstores might have to close because the GST is causing such a drastic drop in sales. Across Canada, publishers report that revenues are down 20 to 30 per cent.
The Coalition against Taxes on Books claims that plunging book sales can be directly attributed to the GST. Canada's magazine industry despairs and publishers are reeling from a triple dose of gloom and doom: recession, impending postal rate increases and the hated GST.
Some time ago the Prime Minister mused publicly that his government would reconsider the wisdom of this tax on literacy, and in the recent Throne Speech the Prime Minister gave his commitment to develop a learning culture and enhance Canadian literacy.
I appeal to the Prime Minister to demonstrate this commitment in a tangible way by seizing this opportunity for action. Repeal the GST on books and magazines immediately and help breathe some life back into the Canadian publishing industry. Stop this unfair and punitive tax.

Madam Speaker, for a few moments yesterday I saw some common sense in politics. It involved the Liberals and the NDP in the Ontario legislature, no Conservatives. When Premier Rae announced that two new ministers had tendered their resignations as a result of each making a mistake, I was pleased and even proud to be a politician when the Liberal leader, Bob Nixon, stood in
his place and suggested that it might be appropriate for Mr. Rae to refuse these resignations. I thought this a common sense approach.
In no other reasonable human endeavour that I know of would someone be required to lose their position for one mistake. There is a difference between mistakes and the intent to do wrong and they should be treated differently.
I applaud Mr. Nixon's first position on this issue because it is the position that most Canadians would take in real life, but then again politics is not much like real life.

Madam Speaker, often the role of our artists is overlooked. Recently, the Professional Association of Canadian Theatres eloquently expressed that role with which I concur and promote.
They said:
Artists are the imagination of a culture, of a country. Through their creative endeavours, artists keep a community in touch with where they have been, where they are and the possibilities for the future.
The government's cuts to Canada's cultural institutions are squeezing the life out of Canada's arts organizations and independent artists. And without artists, who will reflect the unique, diverse, rich experiences in all regions of this country?
As Canada faces the complex challenges of the next millennium, the country needs to further unleash the powers of the artistic imagination, not strangle it.
As theatre artists, we call upon the federal government to reinstate and increase funding to the Canada Council, the National Arts Centre, the CBC, the National Film Board, and Canadian museums. We call upon the government to pay more than lips service to developing a creative vision for Canada.
I add, as a word of warning to this government, in the interest of national unity and Canadian identity-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Two days ago the Minister of Employment and Immigration said the government had been counselled to lie in the Mashat affair. Yesterday, the same minister said that the government had only been counselled to mislead. There is no distinction between lie and mislead.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister confirm to the House whether the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who stated in the press yesterday that the misleading advice was contained in so-called "House cards" advising ministers to respond, and I quote: "Mr. A1 Mashat met the requirements as a retiree, was processed under normal standards, and was not accorded preferential treatment".

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration responded to questions of that nature in the House yesterday, and I believe he responded outside the House. I have nothing further to add.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The Minister of Employment and Immigration has told members of this House and has told the national media that the Government of Canada was counselled to give misleading information to Canadians.
Would the Deputy Prime Minister explain to members of this House exactly what information was the misleading information?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member would have to direct that question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, who unfortunately is not in the House.
Which far away country did you send him to?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
The hon. minister is a member of Parliament and also a cabinet minister. He has important duties to discharge. I think my hon. friend from Newfoundland would understand that.
He did explain the position, and also his poor choice of words as he suggested he may have used, thereby resulting in a misinterpretation. I think that he has come forth in a manner that befits the integrity of the institution and befits his own integrity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the doctrine of ministerial responsibility, as defined by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on May 30 states:
When an error is made of which the minister is unaware, the
minister acts to establish the facts, corrects the error and, in
addition, promises that the offenders will be disciplined and that
their mistakes corrected.
My question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. When the government became aware that a minister had been counselled to mislead the people of Canada, what action did the Government of Canada take against those who counsel such misconduct? Can the Deputy Prime Minister inform the House of the action that was taken? Can he also inform the House what actions have been taken against the senior public servant in this country, Mr. Paul Tellier?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

Madam Speaker, that is precisely what was done. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated in this House that corrective measures were taken so that this kind of issue would not occur again.
The hon. member may have some deviation or some suggestion with respect to how ministerial responsibility should be performed within the context of our parliamentary democracy. I think it is quite clear that the McGrath commission brought down some explicit terms of reference and guidelines, which indeed are followed. If the hon. member has some suggestions to make or wants to pursue the whole issue of ministerial responsibility in the context of parliamentary reform, I suspect

Oral Questions
that that is a suggestion that could very well be put to the Mr. Nunziata: "Scurrying for cover". Will the minister appropriate committee. Perhaps we would be interested of external affairs- in knowing.

I would like to put my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Minister of Immigration said that he was counselled by government officials to lie to Canadians. Was the minister of external affairs counselled to lie to Canadians, and if so, who was it that counselled her?

That has been before the committee. The minister yesterday made his own statement in this regard and there is nothing further to add.

Madam Speaker, is it any wonder that Canadians from one coast to the other do not believe what the government is saying on this particular matter. Is it any wonder that editorial opinion right across the country is condemning this government for its handling of the Al-Mashat matter?
Madam Speaker, referring to cabinet ministers of the government, the Montreal Gazette today says "They behaved more like cockroaches scurrying for cover when the lights-"

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will put his question now, please.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Statistics Canada confirmed again today that inflation is still at 6.2 per cent. What Canadians have known for a very long time is that it is getting tougher and tougher to make ends meet and to put food on the table. While inflation is at 6.2 per cent, wage increases are half of that.
Clearly the government has decided to attack the wrong problem in attacking wage levels. Rather than attacking the wrong problem, why does the minister not do something to get on the right track and bring in real policies, and change policies like the GST, lower the interest rates and get the Canadian dollar down so Canadian families can make ends meet again.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the decline in inflation is encouraging. It has dropped from
6.3	per cent to 6.2 per cent. It is a small decline, but at least it is going in the right direction. I think we should recognize that included in the inflationary figures are the direct and indirect impacts of the various budgets across the country. In this case, this reflects the budgets of Ontario, Quebec and others, which have to be worked through the system.
Yes, as a matter of fact it is the GST and that has been recognized at the very outset. My predecessor indicated and we have confirmed that the GST would indeed have a one-time effect upon inflationary pressures. However, it was important to have this institution put in place for the benefit of our manufacturing industry. I say to the hon. member, who is suggesting we need to have jobs and improve our competitiveness, the GST does just that for the manufacturing sector.

Oral Questions

A supplementary, Madam Speaker. I would suggest to the minister that he should go to some of the border towns across this country and look at the bankruptcy statistics and see how much good his policies have really done for the Canadian economy.
I would address my supplementary to the minister responsible for trade. Since the Canada-U.S. trade deal, Canadian wages have been falling as well, and trade experts now say that the trade deal with Mexico will result in a further decrease in Canadian workers' wages.
I want to ask the Minister responsible for International Trade what assurances he can give Canadian workers that wages will not fall. If he cannot give those assurances, will he stop the negotiations until he can come up with those assurances for the workers of this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not know why the hon. member would draw that conclusion. Since the free trade agreement with the United States came in, Canadian wages have gone up faster than those in the United States. So clearly it does not have anything to do with trade negotiations or trade deals themselves.

Madam Speaker, in Montreal, 200,000 people are out of work. One person out of four is either on unemployment insurance or welfare.
A few weeks ago in Montreal, I met employees in the garment industry. For these employees, free trade with the United States and Mexico will mean more jobs lost, but the government is going ahead regardless.
Will the minister have the decency to talk to these people whose jobs are being threatened, before continuing these talks? Look at the facts!

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it might be of interest to the hon. member if she realized that John Forsythe Canada Limited is looking at the possibility of opening a plant in Mexico. The purpose for that is to transfer jobs from
countries in the Far East into Mexico so they can serve the Canadian market better from Mexico than from places like Taiwan or Hong Kong.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Earlier this week, the Minister of Finance introduced legislation to create the debt reduction fund that was previously announced in the February budget. Will the minister confirm that this debt reduction will itself be in a deficit position of almost $27 billion by the end of the current fiscal year and that after five years, the debt reduction fund will have an accumulated deficit of almost $122 billion? If we reduce the debt at this rate, we could be in big trouble before long.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for that question because he simply demonstrates the magnitude of the problem that we have. Day after day after day, we have the Liberals and the NDP calling for the expenditure of more money. We have got to start putting a discipline on our expenditures.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Well, over 90 per cent of the increase in the debt that has occurred since we have been in office is as a result of the compound interest on the debt that we inherited, and Canadians had better not forget that.
In the days of the Liberals, the annualized increase in program spending was 14 per cent. Under the days of the Tories it was 3.7 per cent. We are exercising fiscal discipline, they did not.

Madam Speaker, I know that 1984 seems like yesterday to the minister, but it is time he started to take account for what he has been doing over the last seven years.
Now that it is clear that the government is going to have to borrow money to finance the debt reduction fund, will the minister admit that this is simply an attempt to use the statement of Public Accounts of Canada as another press line to distract Canadians from the real issue of this government's mismanagement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with those kinds of calculations, it is no wonder that we saw the national debt triple between 1981 and 1984 under the Liberal regime.
The fact of the matter is that it is costing this year $43 billion to pay the cost of servicing the debt. What we are saying is we want to carve out the amount of money that is collected from the GST to apply to that and eventually to apply to the pay-down of the national debt. I hope we have the support of the hon. member opposite, particularly when we bring in legislating spending caps because that will provide further discipline and further integrity and credibility to our program of fiscal consolidation.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
Last December, the President of the Treasury Board released Public Service 2000 as the government's policy for the renewal and revitalization of the Public Service. The lines of responsibility were clearly spelled out as: "Ministers are individually and collectively responsible for the activities of government, including the management and conduct of the Public Service."
Given that the government unanimously voted against the motion affirming its own policy, I ask the minister: If this statement of ministerial responsibility is not the government's policy, what is?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that the position of the government as expressed in the white paper of PS-2000 is absolutely clear.
We have indicated in that white paper the massive changes that we want to bring to the administration of this government, and we are going to do it with the Public Service. I can tell you that after having visited a large number of cities all across Canada, I am convinced that they are in this with us, participating fully.
I can report today that this is progressing, well even though we have a very difficult environment.

Madam Speaker, the minister obviously has no explanation for the conflict between the government's policy and the government's vote on Wednesday.
PS-2000 also says: "Public servants will be empowered
Oral Questions
and encouraged to be innovative, to show greater initiative and greater flexibility. Risk taking will be encouraged and rewarded".
Will the minister admit that in the wake of the Al-Mashat affair, risk taking and innovation are the last things on the minds of Public Servants? Will he admit that PS-2000, to quote Dian Cohen, is "dead in the water"?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will agree to no such thing, because the hon. member knows full well that this is not the case.
She referred to a vote that was taken in this House. She knows it was a vote of confidence. These are usual little tricks that are well understood by us. They may not be understood by everyone, but we know very well that we can read through that.
As for PS-2000,1 can again repeat what I have said. It is proceeding with the full assistance of, I do not know how many thousands of civil servants, I have met. We are working at improving the empowerment.
It is a difficult change to go from a control-oriented organization to a citizen service concerned organization, but we are doing it and it is going on veiy well.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the lie to which the Minister of Immigration referred yesterday was based upon an external affairs house card. I have a copy of that house card, and nowhere is there any lie on that document.

Oral Questions
In view of the fact that the only lie that has been told was on the document which was prepared by the Clerk of the Privy Council, Paul Tellier, when he indicated that Al-Mashat got no preferential treatment, my question to the minister is this.
Was the minister also advised by officials to mislead or lie to Canadians and, if so, by which officials? What action has she taken to follow up on the statements made by her colleague?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all of the things that relate to the house card were made clear in the chronology and were made clear in committee.
They have been available to the public for some time, and I am sure the committee will have its comments to make on them. I do not have anything to add to what my colleague said yesterday or to what I said in committee.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
The minister's colleague yesterday said that he was briefed by external affairs officials to mislead Canadians. My supplementary is very straightforward.
Has she spoken with her colleague? Has she determined which officials briefed her colleague to mislead or lie to Canadians? Was she also briefed the same way?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I find the questions a little difficult in this House, given that all of these issues have been dealt with in committee and it is clear in the chronology. I will be interested to hear what the committee has to say about this. My colleague and I have conferred on any number of aspects of this case, as the hon. member knows, and we have put procedures in place to ensure that this kind of thing does not happen again. That is what we are here to do and that is what we are doing.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Later this day I will be tabling a petition of 50,000 or more signatures from Canadians across the country who are urging the government to remove the goods and services tax from feminine hygiene products.
Given the apparent discriminatory nature of this application of the GST, and since the petition is directed to the Minister of Finance, I will be giving it personally to the Minister responsible for the Status of Women in a few moments.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, will he remove the GST on feminine hygiene products?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. First of all, I don't believe that there is discrimination in the application of feminine hygiene products. As the hon. member knows, the purpose of the GST was to establish a broader base tax at the lowest possible rate. So the GST covers a broad range of goods and services.
It would be very difficult to consider a broad base of exemptions without affecting the actual rate of the GST. So the more exemptions that one would provide, the higher the rate would be. And, so, it would be very difficult to consider that at this particular time.
There are many basic necessities that bear the GST and, while I sympathize with the hon. member in this particular case, it would be very difficult to engage in a broader exemption than that already applied, which is essentially food and medical services.

Madam Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, or perhaps to the Acting Prime Minister.
Approximately 2,500 Canadian men and women will receive their well-deserved volunteer service medals on June 22, a week from tomorrow. These medals are coming from the Canadian government for their contribution to the Persian Gulf war.
Will the minister advise the House why the government cannot at the same time either present or announce when the Canadian men and women who served in the Korean war will receive their well-deserved, distinctly Canadian, volunteer service medals for their contribution in the Korean war on behalf of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can advise the hon. member that that issue is under very active consideration, that is the voluntary Korean service medal. I hope that we will be in a position to announce it in the not too distant future.
I appreciate the hon. member's support in this particular area. I have been personally involved in it and I can assure him that they will be duly recognized, as they should be.

In view of the Deputy Prime Minister's answer, would it be safe to assume that the government is going to look favourably and generously toward these Korean veterans very, very soon? If that is a fair assumption, will there be an announcement soon telling Canadians when the medals will be presented, where they will be presented, by whom, and will medals be presented posthumously to the families of Korean veterans who were killed in Korea or who are since deceased?

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, I am pleased to receive the representation from the hon. gentleman.
I can indicate to him that the whole issue is being studied very closely by the Minister of Veterans Affairs and by the Minister of National Defence. They will be making an announcement to the House as soon as possible and certainly will take on board any representations made by my hon. colleague.

My question is to the Minister of Justice.
As the minister knows, the government co-sponsored and signed the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child; yet in that convention it says that "any child that is deprived of liberty shall be held separate and apart from adults unless it is not in the interests of that child to do so".
Yet this government proceeds to house and jail children and young offenders with adult criminals. This is
Oral Questions
going to be made worse by the government's policies in Bill C-12, the amendments to the Young Offenders Act.
Why does the minister not just admit that the reason the government cannot ratify this convention is that it is prohibited from doing so by the government's own policies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member's reference to the amendments to the Young Offenders Act is not in order for Question Period since it is before the House and he has the opportunity to make his representations there.
I think the hon. member will also recognize that it was his party which brought in the Young Offenders Act and that there are enormous difficulties presented to society in trying to draw distinctions between adult and young offenders and just create a system or regime that is fair and equitable.
I know my colleague, the Solicitor General, has considerable concern about the facilities for the incarceration of all people in Canada who come into violation of the law. I would say that we are very much committed to trying to have a system of justice that does justice to people of all ages in Canada. It is an ongoing preoccupation both with myself and my provincial colleagues to provide the appropriate facilities for young offenders.

Madam Speaker, we finished the legislative hearings on Bill C-58, the predecessor legislation, in December and still we are waiting.
Also when this bill was passed by the former Liberal government it was the intention that young offenders be housed separate and apart from adult criminals.
It has been over a year since this convention was signed and co-sponsored by this government and yet it has not been ratified. I realize that the provinces have to agree, but the provinces also had to agree to housing young offenders separate and apart, which this government has just insisted on letting slide.
Why does the government not admit that it has no intention of fulfilling the mandate of the UN charter on the rights of the child? When, if it does have an intention of signing it, is this very important convention going to be ratified in this country?

Oral Questions

June 14, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member, I am sure, would have noted that the Bank of Canada rate went down four basis points yesterday, which is again probably the 13th or 14th successive decline, and as inflationary pressures recede so will interest rates drop. I think that is the most encouraging note.
Inflationary pressures are receding and the actual inflationary statistics prove that out. It is encouraging to note that it could then follow that interest rates could be reduced further still. At least that is obviously our hope and expectation, but it must be accompanied and it can only happen if we attack the root causes of inflation, the inflationary pressures and the inflationary expectations.
I am sure my hon. friend would welcome the fact that interest rates have declined over the past year by more than 5 percentage points and that the spread between Canadian and U.S. interest rates on three-month commercial paper is about 2.5 per cent. That is a dramatic decline from the 5.6 per cent it was over a year ago.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Attorney General, in the absence of the Solicitor General, and it is about Kitty Nowdluk-Reynolds, an Inuit crime victim.
Ms. Nowdluk-Reynolds was improperly arrested last summer on a material witness warrant. She was then taken in handcuffs from Surrey, B.C. to Edmonton, to Yellowknife, back to Edmonton, to Ottawa and finally to Iqaluit over a nightmare week for a trial at which she was not even called to testify.

In handcuffs?

Oral Questions

In handcuffs. Will she tell us why no official, including herself or the Solicitor General, has until now, 10 months later, made an apology in this matter or done anything to ensure that it will not happen again?

Why have you not done something if it has been that long?

I would agree that it is an extremely important issue. I have in fact taken it under advisement and acted on it. As I said, I welcome the hon. member's somewhat belated interest in this subject.

Madam Speaker, the minister's father is a Crown attorney and has been in British Columbia for many years. I wonder who brought it to her attention.
The only correspondence she has had up until now is a quote from a B.C. RCMP inspector who said: "No matter what you are arrested for, all prisoners are treated the same way".
Does the minister stand by that kind of guff from an inspector? What is-her policy? Is she prepared to have an independent inquiry done, again to repeat, to ensure that this sort of thing does not happen again.

I believe that an inquiry is being made in the RCMP into these activities. Madam Speaker, yesterday the Ontario government announced it will begin negotiations tomorrow on the land claims of the Algonquin Nation of Golden Lake.
The traditional lands of the Golden Lake Algonquins comprise 14,000 square miles of the Ottawa Valley and in fact Parliament Hill, upon which these proceedings are taking place, is a part of unceded Algonquin lands.
In spite of the Prime Minister's trumpeted, new native agenda on land claims and the government's clear interest in the assets of the national capital, the federal government will only be sending an observer to these negotiations without a full mandate to negotiate.
My question to the Deputy Prime Minister is: Why is the federal government refusing to participate fully in negotiations of the Algonquin claim when it could have such profound implications for the Ottawa Valley, for the national capital and for the national interest?
