I know that the minister is as concerned and as interested in this as anybody, and I know he will respond to the member when he returns to the House next week.

Madam Speaker, last summer we saw, within an hour's drive of the capital, the results of the federal government's delay and duplicity in dealing with Mohawk claims.
Aboriginal frustration ultimately resulted in the expenditure of millions of dollars, the loss of Canada's reputation internationally, and the death of a Quebec policeman.
Does the minister not think it important, given the federal government's interest in the national capital area and its jurisdiction over aboriginal affairs, that it should be a full participant in tripartite negotiations with the Algonquin people of Golden Lake?

The government will take whatever action is essential to ensure that land claims right across this country are settled fairly and equitably and with as greatest dispatch as possible.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology.
In its February budget, the government announced it would release a document on Canada's economic prosperity in the spring. Summer starts next week, and we have yet to see this document.
We know that talking about prosperity is embarrassing for this government. Could the minister tell us whether the government still intends to publish this document, and if so, when?

Will the minister admit that this disagreement within the bureaucracy reflects the confusion of its political masters, and that the government does not know what to do to ensure the prosperity of Canada and to provide jobs to Canadians?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the hon. member would look at the policies we have been following as a government, the hon. member would see that they have all been designed on the economics side to improve our competitiveness as a nation and, through that improved competitiveness, build on the prosperity that we all want to see. The range of policies, whether the broad policies of deficit control and inflation control, deregulation, tax reform or other policies related to the more specific areas of the impact on the economy, are all designed to improve the competitive position of the country.
This new document is designed to carry forward from that. There is no confusion whatsoever. There has been a very consistent theme, starting back in 1984 when we were first elected, and carrying us through to this dialogue now, which will set in place the policies that will carry us through to the end of this decade and into the next century.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:

These residents are very concerned about the application that is currently before the CRTC regarding the bid by Unitel Communications for entry into the long distance telephone market.

They are very concerned about the future of postal service in that riding and call upon this government to provide postal service as a service and not as a profit-making venture.
As well, I have a petition from a number of people from the community of Bramalea, also in my riding, who are also concerned about the post office. They have experienced the absence of a post office. service in Bramalea, including access to mail during the winter, confusion about parcel service, and it is causing very serious difficulties with the residents. They call upon this government to put in place a proper postal service for that community.

They call upon this government to give farmers in this country the opportunity to have oats under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board and to protect them by amending the Canadian Wheat Board Act to give oats and barley the same protection as wheat.

By the

a)	Almost 54 per cent of these members belonged to plans to which contributions for plan benefits were provided entirely by the employer (non-contributoiy plans)

b)	The percentage of employees belonging to contributory plans in which the employers finance more than 50 per cent of the required contributions is not known. Madam Speaker, I will wrap up my remarks fairly quickly. One of the things we should be looking at is what the action is of the government in relation to the resources it has to deal with the question of tobacco.
I think we have to put into perspective that this increase in taxes alone, not the total revenue from tobacco taxes, but the increase, will be $1.4 billion in the first year and it will drop down to just under $1 billion a year. Spending, in terms of dealing with this major health issue, should be balanced against that.
For example, this year, it is spending only $3.3 million on the national strategy to reduce tobacco use. That is a very, very small amount, particularly when it is compared with some other expenditures in the health area. It is spending $41 billion on the national drug strategy and $38 million on the AIDS program.
Both of those are worthy programs and I would certainly encourage the government to spend more in those areas. But when you look at the expenditures in the tobacco area of $3.3 million, compared to a $1.4 billion increase in revenue, one really begins to wonder what its priorities are.
Knowing it has this massive revenue to do it, I would like to see the federal government become far more aggressive in the following areas: the promotion of health in general and healthy lifestyles, which is something it could do positively, promote the reduction of the consumption of tobacco, particularly programs aimed at reducing the initial addiction of youth and, third, develop programs to assist those people who are addicted to tobacco to withdraw from tobacco consumption.
We spend many, many millions of dollars on drug treatment centres, drug counselling, but as a national government, we spend almost nothing to assist people who are addicted to cigarette smoking to withdraw.
It could spend money on health research. In the last two years the government has dramatically reduced its expenditures on health research at a time when we should be increasing expenditures. These are areas in which it could use this massive increase in revenue, $1.4 billion, to do something positive.

The last area should be pursued aggressively. It should be assisting farmers and workers in the tobacco area in positive adjustment programs by assisting the tobacco growers to develop alternative crops and markets for those crops and tobacco workers to develop adjustments and training programs so they can go into other types of employment. Let us remind ourselves, they have an increase in revenue of $1.4 billion so they can do it.
This type of approach has tremendous public support. Environics polled Canadians to find out what kind of support there was for using the increase in tobacco revenues in various areas. They found out that 84 per cent supported its use in research into disease. Another 84 per cent supported its use in preventing smoking among young people. Seventy-eight per cent supported its use in helping people quit smoking and the same number supported the use of that money to promote healthier lifestyles.
It is quite interesting that one of the things the public did not support the use of this money for was to reduce the debt.
In other words, the public sees this as a health tax not as a revenue tax. It does not want it used as revenue for the government to try to reduce its deficit or reduce the impact of its fiscal mismanagement on the economy. The public is quite prepared to support it as a health tax.
I guess, I and my New Democratic colleagues would also support it on this basis and that is why we support this government's legislation.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague for the excellent presentation he made on this issue.
As you know, I have made a number of presentations before in this House in an attempt to reduce the amount of smoking this addictive substance that takes place in Canada, and I certainly strongly support the increase that is proposed for the excise tax on cigarettes and tobacco products.
But I believe, as my colleague believes, that this tax should not be called an excise tax because it leads people
Government Orders
to believe that this is simply something that goes into the national treasuiy and, like everything else that seems to go into the national treasury, disappears from view from the point of view of public programs.
Maybe there is an opportunity in committee stage to label this tax as a supplementary medicare premium, because, as my colleagues who have spoken on this issue have pointed out during the debate, smoking costs thousands of lives throughout Canada. It also damages the health of many tens of thousands of Canadians and, as a result of that loss of life and as a result of that damage to health, it incurs the expenditure of hundreds of millions of Canadian tax dollars on things like health and hospital care. Those have to be shouldered, not simply by smokers, but by all Canadians.
If we had a supplementary medical premium attached to cigarettes instead of calling it excise taxes then people would get a clear grasp as to what the problem is in this case.
I do hope, as well, that the government will carry on this philosophy into other areas. It should stop subsidizing the growing of tobacco and stop subsidizing tobacco advertising through the tax system. It should gradually phase out the import and the export of tobacco products from Canada. It should establish adjustment programs that will assist farmers who are currently involved in growing tobacco to shift to other crops. Also it should help workers who are involved in the tobacco industry at the current time so that they can leave that industry with retraining and other programs and not experience any loss of income or socioeconomic standing.
So I congratulate the speakers who have spoken today on the viewpoints they have presented and I certainly congratulate my colleague from Surrey North for the excellent information that he has given to this House.

Madam Speaker, I must say that the member's very imaginative idea of having this tax designated as a health tax or a health premium would be in line with the feelings of the Canadian public because the surveys and polling on this clearly indicate that the public supports this when the money is directed towards the health of the public, including preventing young people

Government Orders
from smoking, helping people to quit smoking and promoting healthier lifestyles.
But, at the same time, the public does not support its use to reduce the deficit or to replace the advertising revenues for sports organizations that tobacco companies are now doing in promotions.
There is one other very interesting thing that I think relates to this. The public not only does not like this money being swallowed up into the government's revenues, it clearly said that it felt independent, non-government bodies should be responsible for the expenditure of these dollars. I think that is an indication of the lack of confidence that Canadians now have in the wisdom of the expenditures of this government.
So the public is saying that it supports the idea of a health tax, but it thinks the expenditures should be under the control of somebody we can reliably trust.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to voice my strong objections to Bill C-10, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and Excise Act.
Let us be clear about this bill. The government has attempted to cloud the issue and cover up the real intent of this bill. This is nothing more than a tax bill, a tax grab.
This bill proposes a 3 cent per cigarette increase in the federal excise tax and, by its own estimates, this increase will mean an additional $1.4 billion in the federal government's coffers.
The real intent of this bill is to increase the government's revenue, not to help the health of Canadians. Its aim is nothing more than to take money from the pockets of ordinary Canadians. It is a regressive tax. It is an unfair tax and it is an unnecessary tax.
I,	as the spokesperson for Haldimand-Norfolk, want to tell this government that the people of Haldimand- Norfolk oppose this tax. I am opposed because what it will not do is encourage people to stop smoking as much as it will encourage them to get their cigarettes elsewhere, to cross-border shop or to buy smuggled or stolen cigarettes.
I am opposed to this bill because coupled with this government's abandonment of transition programs, it leaves tobacco farmers high and dry.
This is not a health bill. The government certainly has a right and a responsibility to show its view on smoking and to alert Canadians to the potential health risks of smoking. That is not what is at issue here.
What is at issue here is the use of the tax system to impose an incredible burden on Canadians who supposedly considered these warnings and exercised their ultimate right to choose to smoke.
The government is concerned about the young starting to smoke. It should be implementing programs like the one in the United States in which starting in the first grade students enter a program educating them on the dangers of smoking and offering certificates for the completion of this program.
In a recent article, Herbert Laframboise, a former Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare says that this U.S. program will give students a "continuous bombardment as to the ills and dangers of smoking and would be the nucleus of a smoke-free society." According to Laframboise, one reason this deterrence program is not pursued by the government as an alternative to raising taxes is that "it costs money and it does not generate revenue".
I welcome any government's concern for the health of Canadians, but I think its concern should not be limited to those matters which will just fatten its own coffers.
It strikes me as a little bit ironic that this government on the one hand attempts to pass off major tax grabs as a health measure when it closes its eyes to other major health programs or other major health concerns facing Canadians.
I am thinking of the real concern posed by the additive MMT now being used in Canadian gas. The members opposite must surely be aware of the significant health danger posed by MMT. Its dangers have been brought to their attention numerous times by my colleague, the member for Lambton-Middlesex.
The U.S. banned MMT in unleaded gas in 1978. A subcommittee of the House energy commerce committee in the United States wrote last year a letter to the Environmental Protection Agency which said: "We are extremely concerned about the substantial serious health impacts from the introduction of MMT gasoline. Manganese is listed as an air toxic capable of serious neuro toxic effects".

This government knows this and yet it does nothing about it. I urge the government to address all the serious health concerns facing Canadians, including the use of MMT, and not to limit its health concerns only to those which will enable it to justify a $5 billion tax grab.
Tobacco consumption rates in Canada have declined. Cigarette consumption in Canada has fallen from $63 billion in 1983 to $47 billion in 1989. This decline is due to rising health concerns, government smoking regulations and taxes.
According to Mr. Laframboise:
Many of the people who have quit have been people whose attachment to smoking has not been strong.
A surprising number of former smokers smoked casually as a social habit, and for reasons yet to be explained, never became addicted to nicotine.
Mr. Laframboise then goes on to talk about the people who are not so lucky, those who are addicted to nicotine. He writes: "It is these hard cases who are most trapped and punished by high taxes on tobacco. They are smokers of relative long-standing. Burdening them with the present level of taxes can fairly be described as a cruel exploitation of a population addicted to a legal product".
Tobacco farmers have been equally exploited by this government. With this latest tax increase the government will be collecting over $4 billion a year in tobacco taxes; $4 billion a year from the sweat and labour of my tobacco farmers. What part of this $4 billion-plus has it given back to tobacco farmers this year to help them cope with what is for many of them a loss of livelihood? Nothing. Absolutely nothing.
Last March, this government stopped accepting applications for the REDUX program which helps farmers exit the tobacco industry. There are now over 600 tobacco farmers on the waiting list for the program, even though it ran out of money months ago. The government has yet to allocate any new money for this program. Tobacco farmers are hanging on to a financial shoestring and this government is content to leave them twisting in the wind.
The same sad story of this abandonment of tobacco farmers is told by the government's handling of the Alternative Enterprise Initiative. This program was designed to help farmers find alternative crops to tobacco. It ran out of money months ago and the government is giving no clue as to its future. A tobacco farmer with 18 acres produces about 45,000 pounds of dried production of which the farmer's gross revenue before cost is $66,000. Of that, this government makes a tax profit of
Government Orders
$4.5 million. That is 68 times what the farmer makes on his own product.
Per package, the farmer's revenue is 7.3 cents. The federal government's tax revenue is $2.31 and the provincial government Ontario's revenue for instance, is $2.04, $4.35 in Ontario alone.
Since 1984, 900 farmers have abandoned tobacco leaving about 1,200 attempting to hang on. The transition has been very large and very rapid. Nowhere has this rapid transition and displacement been felt more strongly than in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk, which traditionally has been one of the largest tobacco growing regions in the country.
Many farmers have lost their farms. Some have struggled to start anew with a different crop, buying different tools and equipment, learning a new crop and usually taking a loss for the first few years. There are only so many farmers who can find a new crop without flooding the market and very few have actually succeeded.
Farmers are a vital part of the economy of Haldimand-Norfolk, and of Canada, and when they suffer the people of Haldimand-Norfolk suffer. The people of Canada suffer. The comer stores that used to supply farmers with their groceries suffer. The small businesses where the farmer used to buy his tools suffer. The students who worked in the fields and needed money to continue their education suffer. All Canadians suffer.
After collecting billions of dollars each year from the labours of these hard working farmers and Canadians, the government is now putting them in a situation in which they cannot leave the tobacco industry without losing their farms and retirement funds. Even when this government had in past years allocated money to these programs, the funding was woefully inadequate. For every $300 it collected from tobacco it gave less than $1 back to farmers who had produced it and had lost their livelihood. Now this government contents itself with stalling tactics and the continuation of these nickel and dime programs.
The Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Marketing Board has worked long and hard to receive just treatment for the tobacco farmers from the federal government. They have asked the government countless times to end the ad hoc, piecemeal approach to tobacco compensation and, yet now, when the entire state of tobacco is uncertain, this government even refuses to give the board any indication what compensation farmers leaving the industry will receive this year.

Government Orders
Imagine the uncertainty and the stress this lack of government compassion is causing the stricken farmers this very minute. These farmers want nothing more than to be treated fairly.
This is the same government whose current Minister of Finance and former Minister of Agriculture said to tobacco farmers in my riding two and a half years ago, just before the election: I quote:
Ottawa wants to send a strong signal to the industry that we are
here to support tobacco producers in their time of need and
adjustment.
I ask this government and I ask the minister: What happened to this promise?
The people of Haldimand-Norfolk feel betrayed by this government.
As a last resort, some tobacco farmers have joined together in defiance and disillusionment. Some 950 farmers, 30 share growers and 20 small business owners have joined together to file a law suit against the federal and provincial governments. They call themselves FACT, Fair Compensation for Tobacco. Under the leadership of Fred Homeniuk, they are seeking justice in our courts where they have not received it from our governments.
Mr. Homeniuk says the law suit is, and I quote: "An attempt to regain our dignity".
They want to know whether the governments have a constitutional right to tax a legal product to the extent that its growers are deprived of their right to earn a livelihood and to gain just compensation.
How did our governments respond to their quest? They tried to have FACT'S lawsuit thrown out of court before it was even heard. Luckily, the government's attempt has failed and the lawsuit is proceeding.
Farmers are not the only ones fed up with this government's tax grabs. Canadians have responded to the current campaign against unfair tobacco taxes with an enthusiasm that could only be a result of a deep-felt anger and frustration.
The tax protest forms being mailed to the Prime Minister, which I understand are sitting a room in the
Langevin Block and not even being read by the Prime Minister, say:
I am of voting age. I want you to stop unfair taxation of tobacco
products in Canada. What are you going to do about it? I expect a
reply.
In the first two weeks of the campaign alone, 453,600 protest cards have been processed. Depending on the province a Canadian lives in, 70 to 80 per cent of the cost of a typical $6 package of cigarettes is tax. For a pack-a-day smoker in Ontario, taxes amount to $1,599 a year.
When taxation reaches excessive levels, black market activity flourishes and Canadian cigarettes are no exception.
Recent studies show that last year, an estimated 11 million cartons of stolen cigarettes were fenced in Canada. According to officials, cigarette theft has risen sharply since the latest tax hike which is the subject of the bill being implemented today and talked about today.
A recent article in the Western Report says: "Criminals, always responsive to the demands of the marketplace, are stealing cigarettes at an unprecedented rate". Calgary sees an average of six robberies a day involving cigarettes.
In February, 13 people were caught as they attempted to steal $3.6 million worth of cigarettes hijacked from two CP Rail trains.
In March, two thieves hit a wholesale warehouse, held a clerk at gunpoint and escaped with $25,000 worth of cigarettes. "Cigarettes are the hottest target around right now", says Calgary Police Superintendent Gerry Baxter.
The smuggling of cigarettes across the Canada-U.S. border has risen dramatically since this latest tax increase.
A recent study done by Peat Marwick Thome finds:
This additional tax burden effectively increases the demand for the
smuggled product to avoid the significant tax burden.
Ray Thibault, an intelligence and interdiction officer with Customs Canada says: There's been a definite increase in seizures in the last three months."

The Peat Marwick Thorne study quotes law enforcement estimates of a 10 per cent to 20 per cent increase in cigarette smuggling in the last few months. The study estimates the loss in tax revenue from increased smuggling caused by this tax increase will cost the federal government $30 million.
The differential between Canadian and U.S. tax rates has become so large that smuggling and cross-border shopping are causing real damage to the Canadian economy. On the British Columbia-Montana divide, each package of Canadian cigarettes has $3.06 more tax in its price than its U.S. counterpart. On the Ontario-Michigan border, the additional tax burden on cigarettes is $2.93 per package. In comparing New Brunswick and its border state, Maine, Canadian cigarettes have $3.59 more tax per package.
Our tax rates on cigarettes are inviting Canadians to head down to the U.S. to buy them. They stand to save $20 to $30 off the price of a carton of cigarettes alone. That would more than cover the gas used to get there for most Canadians.
Besides, while they are down there they can fill up their tank and they can save another bundle. And while they are down there, who knows what else they will buy which they might otherwise have bought in Canada, in fact, within my own riding, which is an hour's drive from the border.
There are winners and losers with any piece of government legislation. I oppose this bill because I have problems in it with who wins and who loses.
The winners with this bill are the federal government's coffers, U.S. cigarette retailers, tobacco smugglers and thieves. The losers are law-abiding Canadian taxpayers who smoke and law-abiding, hard-working Canadian tobacco farmers, manufacturers and workers.
It is because of the serious oversights and inadequacies of this bill that I intend to propose amendments in committee and at third reading stage.
I will seek to amend this bill so that tobacco farmers are no longer made the scapegoats of this government. I will propose that the $1.4 billion in additional revenue per year that this government collects from this latest tax hike be given back to the tobacco producers so that those who wish to leave can do so without losing their farms or without losing their pensions and those who wish to stay can have a sustainable industry in which to produce.
Government Orders
I will propose that this government, in conjunction with this tax hike, commit itself to informing tobacco farmers on a 10-year basis of its plans for tobacco tax increases so that they will no longer be the victims of ad hoc increases and will know what their future holds.
Madam Speaker, I see my time is up and I want to send one final message to this government. Canadians will not stand for these tax increases hedged in health legislation. As a matter of fact, Canadians are fed up with this government and their increased tax bills.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to take a couple of short minutes to respond to the member and address some of the concerns that he has raised.
First of all, I think it is very important to note that concerns about the serious health hazards of smoking and recognition of the significant contribution that taxation can make in addressing the problem were the key factors in the government's decision to increase tobacco taxes in this budget.
It is expected that the consumption of cigarettes and other tobacco products will decline by about 9 per cent in the next fiscal year as a result of the increases in tobacco taxes proposed in this legislation and other government initiatives to reduce tobacco use in Canada.
I think it is important to note that higher cigarette prices are particularly effective in discouraging young Canadians from starting to smoke. A 10 per cent increase in price will reduce consumption by young Canadians as much as 14 per cent.
Will Osier advises me that as a result of the tax increases announced in this budget, it is estimated that
100,000	fewer young Canadians will smoke.
I can appreciate the concerns of the member for Haldimand-Norfolk who just spoke. He represents a tobacco producing area. The government has also addressed that concern. As part of its comprehensive strategy to reduce tobacco consumption in Canada, the government established the Tobacco Assistance Program several years ago to assist tobacco producers to leave the industry and to encourage economic diversification of tobacco regions. As a result of federal and provincial assistance, nearly half of all the tobacco farmers in Canada have left the tobacco growing industry over the past five years.

Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I am the member for Haldimand-Norfolk, not Northumberland.
I am somewhat surprised, to tell you the truth, at his comments. Had he been able to talk to the two members on his side from tobacco growing areas, the member for Oxford and the member for Elgin, and had they been in the House to tell him, they might have told him that in fact, the money has run out for the specific programs which he just talked about.
The fact of the matter is that there is no money this year to help tobacco fanners exit tobacco. The fact of the matter is that there is no money this year to help the alternative enterprise initiative and to help farmers divert into other initiatives.
I want to say to the hon. member that before he gets up in the House and spiels off the government lines, he might want to talk to the members from Elgin and Oxford when they get back to this Chamber.

Madam Speaker, I always find myself quite amazed when the Liberal Party can stand up and passionately debate both sides of the issue. But after two or three years in this House, I guess I should no longer be surprised because that is normally the Liberal stand.
They are good at that.

I would also like to say to the member that he forgot to mention the losers, the 35,000 Canadians who die every year. What about their families, their loved ones, their parents, their children? Those are the losers.
You pretend there is no connection between the increase in the price and the reduction of smoking and yet it has been clearly demonstrated that there has been. The only place I would agree with you is in your discussion about the negligence of the Conservative government concerning adjustment programs as they relate to farmers. They could take that $1.4 million and guarantee that there is no sustainable tobacco industry in
Canada. That should be our goal, that there will never be any sustainable tobacco industry in this country.

Madam Speaker, I take exception to the member for Surrey North for challenging my right to stand up for my constituents in this House. I thank God I have a leader who allows me to stand and represent my constituents.
My constituents are concerned about this. They know that this is nothing more than a tax grab couched in health legislation. When that hon. member allows his leader, and when the Prime Minister allows his members to stand up in this House to speak out on behalf of their constituents, then maybe this House will be a better place for all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I should encourage my colleague not to be too surprised. The member for Surrey North often demonstrates that Marxist/Leninism is alive and well in the NDP. In any event, I share the concern that he has expressed.
I want to say first of all, though, that I support the approach to encouraging non-consumption of damaging substances through taxation. I think that has been proven, as has been said, to be a successful strategy.
What concerns me in this legislation is two things, one of which the member called to mind, the historic alliance that existed in Ontario between the temperance movement and the bootleggers, who had a mutual interest in trying to exclude alcohol. The concern we should have is that at a certain level, taxation as a deterrent stands to benefit others than those whose health is being affected by the consumption of tobacco.
The other thing that concerns me-I see it in the budget which I have in front of me-is that when you look through the budget, it is very hard to accept the premise that this is merely a health tax.
The budget highlights the desperate financial position that the Government of Canada is in. It says that one of the fundamental problems is the state of the public finances. It sets out the need to create the Debt Reduction Fund which is going to be in a deficit position itself of $122 billion within five years.
Then it reveals the tobacco tax which will generate over the course of four years, according to the budget, over $4.5 billion, none of which is going to any of the

programs either for encouragement of non-consumption or for adjustment for the tobacco farmers.
I would like the member for Haldimand-Norfolk to respond if he would do that. I find it surprising, since he is not the only member in this House from a tobacco producing area, that nobody else, particularly on the other side of the House seems to be raising the concerns of the farmers in this situation.

Madam Speaker, it is funny where the morality in this House comes from sometimes.
I want to thank the hon. member for his comments. The Minister of Agriculture is sitting in the House now. I know he is new to his portfolio, so he might take some of my comments back to the people in his department and get them moving on this.
Frankly, if he is going to take the line on that side that he does not want tobacco in this country and he does not want smokers in this country, he might be well to help move some of these farmers out of tobacco. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture has discussed this with his officials.
I just want to say to my hon. friend that he is right. It is nothing more than a tax grab. If this government really wanted to stop smoking in Canada, particularly young people, why is it not outlawed? Why does it not do a number of other things that can stop people from smoking in Canada? This is nothing more than a tax grab. The government knows it.

Madam Speaker, I too am somewhat amazed at the defence of the tobacco industry. Certainly when we put in the program to help tobacco producers to change professions, that was their opportunity to get out of this business of selling death.
As far as I am concerned, I think the overwhelming evidence is that public costs for tobacco are outrageous. The government can simply look at the health care budget, but there are other budgets that have to be looked at as well. Indeed, when one looks at the public maintenance budgets around this place, when one looks at the floors, when one looks at any kind of public building, there are enormous costs. We see fires. There are many fires created through cigarette smokers and so on. I particularly find the health costs to be odious but those other costs are public costs as well.
Government Orders
If this was a drug that was being considered for introduction today, it would be banned. There is no question about that. There is tremendous public cost and no value at all. It does not help smokers relax. It does not help them to do anything. It is an addiction that even smokers do not want to have.
What I find particularly insidious is this campaign suggesting that smokers are being encouraged to send in protest documents. What tobacco producers and protest companies are doing is putting in another insidious campaign that is associating smoking with rebellion, particularly against government.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, nothing would have given me greater pleasure today than to be able to rise at this time and inform hon. members that a negotiated settlement had been reached in the grain handling dispute on Canada's west coast.
Unfortunately, that is not the case. I find that instead I must address the House in the context of introducing legislation to bring about a resumption of grain handling operations in the port of Vancouver.
The introduction of such legislation is necessary in order to ensure that economic hardships placed on Canada's agricultural producers as a result of the work stoppage be removed and the country's reputation as a reliable exporter of grain not be placed in jeopardy.
Most hon. members will be aware that the labour dispute in question involves the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators' Association representing five grain elevator companies in the port of Vancouver and the Grain Workers' Union, Local 333, representing some 650 grain workers.
The previous collective agreement between the two parties expired on December 31, 1989 and the parties met in direct negotiations between February and November 1990 in an effort to arrive at a new contract. Despite these efforts, the two sides were unable to reach agreement and a conciliation officer from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service of Labour Canada was appointed on December 4,1990 to assist the parties in resolving their differences.
Even with the provision of third party assistance the association and the union were unable to find a common ground to settle the dispute.
Following the receipt of the report of the conciliation officer, I notified the parties of my decision not to appoint a conciliation commissioner or establish a conciliation board.
As hon. members are aware, the collective bargaining process provided for under Part I of the Canada Labour Code places the onus on the bargaining parties to make the required compromises to arrive at a mutually acceptable solution to their differences.
In not actioning this particular dispute, I indicated to the two sides that I expected them to make their responsibilities seriously and to make the process work for them as opposed to relying on the government to get them off the hook.

Government Orders

In May 1991, the parties met in direct negotiations but failed to make any progress. On May 8, the Grain Workers' Union prohibited its members from working overtime. During the period from May 30 to June 4, the parties met before a mediator from the private sector, Mr. Vince Ready, who subsequently withdrew from the dispute, indicating that the positions of the two parties on the matter at issue were too far apart for the mediation process to proceed normally.
After the mediator left, work slowdowns occurred at a number of grain elevators, and on June 10, the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators' Association locked out workers at all its facilities.

Given the serious consequences of such a work stoppage action I instructed two senior officials of the federal Mediation and Conciliation Service to travel to Vancouver and meet with the parties in order to fully assess the situation. Michael McDermott, Senior Assistant Deputy Minister, and Warren Edmondson, Director General of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service met with the two sides in Vancouver on June 12 and conveyed to them my strongest possible concerns over their failure to resolve their contract dispute.
The parties were also made aware that the government was not prepared to sit back and watch grain exports from the west coast be paralysed by a lengthy work stoppage.
They were also aware that the government was not prepared to tolerate the economic cost to western Canadian farmers, to suffer the potential loss in grain sales and to allow Canada's international reputation as a reliable supplier to suffer.
Despite these urgings, the parties still were not prepared to make the necessary compromises to bring about a resolution of the differences impeding a settlement of a contract dispute. Following consultations with my officials, I have come to the conclusion that there is virtually no prospect of the two sides resolving this conflict in the foreseeable future.
As I have indicated, this government is not prepared to passively stand on the sidelines and witness the tremendous damage which a stoppage of this magnitude is capable of inflicting on the country's economy.
Therefore, I am confident that hon. members on both sides of the House will understand that, while regrettable, the introduction of the British Columbia Grain Handling Operations Act is an action being taken by this government on behalf of all Canadians.
The proposed legislation before the House makes reference to two grain handling disputes. As I have indicated, the dispute between the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators Association and the Grain Workers Union, Local 333, is currently at the lock-out stage.
Hon. members will know that the other dispute referenced in the bill involves Prince Rupert Grain Limited and the Grain Workers Union, also Local 333, and is currently at the conciliation officer stage. This dispute, however, bears similarities to the terminal elevator operations dispute in that the issues for the most part are analogous. Part II of the legislation, if proclaimed, enforced by Order in Council, would provide for resolution of the dispute through the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator.
Of course, we would only seek proclamation of this part if the parties remain unable to settle their own differences and a work stoppage seriously affecting the movement of export grains were to ensue.
Part I of the proposed legislation provides for the immediate resumption of grain handling operations in the port of Vancouver and provides for the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator to deal with all matters remaining in dispute between the parties. The bill extends the term of the collective agreement to include the period beginning January 1, 1990 and extending to December 31, 1991.
Under the terms of the legislation, the mediator-arbitrator is given 90 days, or such longer period as the minister may allow, to endeavour to mediate all of the matters in dispute. In the event that the mediator-arbitrator appointed under the legislation is unable to bring about agreement on any such matter he or she is required to render an arbitral award on the issue.

June 14, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House does not preclude agreement by the parties to amend any provision of the agreement, excepting the one setting the term of the agreement. The bill also contains provisions obliging both parties to comply with the legislation.

The British Columbia Grain Handling Operations Act, while bringing about an end to the current work stoppage, does provide the parties with an alternative to an imposed settlement. By providing for the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator the legislation presents the two sides of the grain handling dispute with a further opportunity to avail themselves of neutral third party assistance in arriving at an acceptable solution to their differences.
I urge the negotiators for the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators Association and the Grain Workers Union to seize this occasion and make every effort to reach an accommodation on the outstanding issues in dispute.
For the information of hon. members the main issues in dispute during this round of negotiations involve wage parity with the west coast longshoremen, continuous operations and employer contributions to the pension plan. These issues are not new to the bargaining relationship between these parties.
While there has been no work stoppage at the Vancouver terminal elevators since 1974, labour peace has often been maintained by setting critical issues aside for further study. Such has been the case with the overtime hours of work issue that underlies the current employer demand for continuous operations. This issue has actually been discussed in one form or another since 1971. In both the 1982 and 1984 bargaining rounds conciliation commissioners recommended further examination and established procedures accordingly. However, the procedures were not followed up in any meaningful fashion and the issue has been left unresolved.
Hon. members may question why the proposed legislation does not contain a provision for a specific study of the continuous operations question, the key issue in the current dispute.
All of the outstanding issues in dispute are essentially of an economic nature and as such they cannot be separated from one another in the legislation. However, should the need for an in depth review of this issue become apparent during the course of the mediation arbitration proceedings, and if the mediator arbitrator asks, I will certainly be happy to give whatever assistance Labour Canada can offer.
As I indicated in my earlier remarks, it is not a pleasant task for me as Minister of Labour to introduce such legislation. However, the parties in this dispute have had ample opportunity, including extensive third party assistance, to resolve the issues in dispute and have failed to do so. They have imposed the consequences of their dispute on the western grain producers, while continuing to reject every opportunity for a settlement through accepted dispute resolution mechanisms.
This government has an obligation to act to protect not only the economic interests of the agricultural sector of this country, but also Canada's reputation as a reliable grain exporter. This legislation serves as evidence of the government's acceptance of that responsibility.
In closing, I would like to thank the members of the government's agricultural caucus for their support of this action today and particularly the hon. Minister of Agriculture and the hon. Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no joy in the immediate task before us. There is no glory to be sought here. There is no joy for me in this bill and there is no joy for my party in this bill. There is no joy because we have far too much respect for collective bargaining, too much respect for workers and their rights and too much respect for grain farmers. There is no joy in stepping in where collective bargaining has failed. There is no joy in forced solutions.
We are called upon to carry out our duty and carry it out we will. Our duty, as we see it, is to restore grain handling services at the port of Vancouver. Our duty, as we see it, is to support the bill before us and secure the re-opening of grain handling facilities at Vancouver.
Allow me to offer a personal perspective. I have been a member of a union. I have had the honour of being a president of a union. I have a great respect for workers and their rights and I have great reluctance to interfere in the exercise of those rights. They have fought long and
June 14 , 1991

hard for what they have got and no one on this side of the House wants to see a diminution of those rights.
I also have a profound respect for farmers, my father was one. My family farmed. I spent my youth on a farm. I know, as we all do on this side of the House, the current precarious situation of farmers. We know how reliant they are on international markets. We know how important it is for them to get their grain through the port of Vancouver. Farmers are near the close of their current crop year. They are busy moving out the grain in preparation for yet another harvest.
I am tom, as I am sure we all are, but we cannot shirk our responsibilities. The Vancouver port must be reopened. I shant chronicle all the events leading up to the current stalemate. Suffice it to say that the grain handlers have worked without contract for about 18 months. Negotiations, along with conciliation, have gone on for months, yet the two sides are no closer on the thorny issues of wages and converting the grain handling facilities into a full blown, seven day operation. There is a deadlock. There is a stalemate. We are persuaded that the port must re-open now so that the grain can get moving again.
Our hope is that the government will name the mediator arbitrator, as provided for in this bill, and that the government will appoint that person very quickly so that he or she can begin the difficult job of finding a solution to this very difficult problem. The existing lock-out began last Monday and the effects of that lock-out have been dramatic. I would like to put it into perspective.
At the present time there are 21 vessels waiting to be loaded in the port of Vancouver, 35 are to arrive by June 30. Exports through the port of Vancouver for the month of April totalled 1.7 million metric tonnes, in May it was
1.6	million metric tonnes. The forecast for the month of June is 1.6 million metric tonnes, for July a little over 2 million metric tonnes, and in August 1.6 million metric tonnes.
There was a slowdown in work at the port before the lock-out occurred. The actual number of cars unloaded in the week ending May 11 was 2,908. The target for that
Government Orders
period was actually 3,550. In the week ending May 18 the actual unloading of cars was 3,191 while the target was 3,550. That story can be told all the way through the month of May and into the month of June.
Of course now with the lock-out there is nothing, nothing going through the port. That means that the port is losing about 54,000 metric tonnes a day-54,000 metric tonnes. To put it in dollar terms, that is about $7 million a day lost by the agricultural economy in western Canada. That is an enormous economic hardship.
We all know the significance of agriculture in the Canadian economy, particularly in western Canada. Farm cash receipts for 1991 were set at $21.7 billion. Farm exports have made up between 40 and 50 per cent of cash farm receipts and 8 per cent of Canada's total exports in 1990.
Approximately 70 to 80 per cent of wheat sales, 65 per cent of canola and 40 per cent of barley comprise a major part of total farm exports. At last count there were
459,000	jobs in the primary farm sector. In the food processing sector, the second largest in the country, there were at last count 225,000 jobs, worth about $43 billion to the economy. Of the 250,000 farms in Canada, cash crop farmers make up 52 per cent.
We all know the precarious situation of the farm economy. The realized net farm income in 1991 is forecast to drop by 22.5 per cent, compared to 1990. Saskatchewan will drop 145 per cent, Alberta 43 per cent, and Manitoba 35 per cent. This reduction in total net farm income is mainly the result of low international grain prices and a dramatic reduction in the federal support programs over the last two years.
A lot of Canadians do not realize that, despite the fact that the average income of farm families is a little over $37,000, 55 per cent of that income actually is derived from income made off the farm.
One more indicator which demonstrates the difficult times down on the farm these days is the number of bankruptcies. In Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta from January 1, 1990 to March 31, 1990 there were 113 bankruptcies. In the same period for 1991 that figure has soared to 140.

Government Orders
When all is said and done, we believe that the case for immediate resumption of grain shipments through the port of Vancouver is compelling. We believe that this bill is veiy, very necessary. I want to touch on a couple of other things. The bill includes a provision to include the terminal at Prince Rupert. As you know, there are labour difficulties there as well. It is possible the same thing may happen in Prince Rupert. The government is proposing that it applies this law to the terminal at Prince Rupert. We have some grave problems with that and we will pursue that in just a few moments when the bill moves on to report stage.
Another thing, this bill in effect asks parliamentarians to be the deciders. That causes concern for us because we really wonder if parliamentarians are the best deciders in a case like this. I would like to ask the government, particularly the hon. Minister of Labour to look at this situation, at possible legislation that will rid parliamentarians of this particular kind of responsibility. At least there should be some kind of probe or investigation to see if there is a better model or system to obviate the need for parliamentarians to be put into this kind of role.
In conclusion, I want to say that the grain must get moving to the port of Vancouver for the sake of farmers, the farm economy, and the whole Canadian economy. The port of Vancouver must be reopened. We support the bill and urge its immediate passage.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the grain workers' union and the B.C. terminal elevator operators are faced with legislation after having been at the bargaining table for 18 months. I think it is important that in beginning this discussion we are very clear that the union did not strike, the employers did.
The union is aware of the needs of the farmers in this country and aware of the needs or the wants of the employer. But in this dispute there appear to be two solitudes. The farmers in Saskatchewan who are barely surviving for earning $2.50 a bushel for their wheat, which is likely to go down to $1.75 a bushel in the next couple of days, and who, in 1947, were earning $2 a bushel for their wheat.
The grain workers in 1947 worked 12-hour days and a 48-hour week. The employers at the elevators in Vancouver are demanding that the union return to the 12-hour day, 48-hour week.
Mr. Speaker, it might be of interest to you, the hon. minister, and other hon. members in this House to know that in 1948, the newly founded Grain Workers' Union struck for six months, without strike pay, to win the 8-hour day, the 40-hour week.
Six months is a long time for a family to survive without income, no income for six months to earn the 8-hour day, 40-hour week. Today the union is asked to turn its back on something for which tremendous sacrifices were made. Moms could not put food on the table. Children were going to school hungry. People were being evicted because they could not pay their rent. They were on strike without strike pay.
Some might ask why the farmers should care about that. It happened in 1947. In fact, the farmers today are fighting a terrible struggle just to survive on their farms. On the other hand the other solitude might ask why the grain workers should care about the farmers who are heavily subsidized anyway.
I believe that the grain workers and the farmers do both care about each other. Many grain workers come from farming backgrounds, and from the prairies.
Many, many, of the farmers whom we are talking about have relatives who are working at the terminals. I believe that both the workers and the farmers are the victims. They are victims of this government's inadequate grain marketing policies.
The price is down largely because of the dispute between the European Economic Community and the U.S. In particular, the Americans have been directly subsidizing grain sales into traditional Canadian markets. To retain markets, the Canadian Wheat Board has had to slash prices. The shipping delay caused by this dispute will cost farmers $9 million a week.
We need a government which will concern itself with promoting the viability of farm families and rural communities at the same time as it concerns itself with promoting good industrial relations in this country.
We also need an industrial relations climate which will ensure that for the grain workers, and other workers in federal jurisdiction, there is a reason to bargain. We have the proof of that need in this bill. If the union strikes, it will be legislated back to work. If the employer strikes, it will be legislated back to work. No one needs to bargain.

I think it is time that this Parliament says: "Parliament should not be the labour court or tribunal of Canada". It is time we look at the process and say that labour legislation must provide a forum for free, good faith collective bargaining in the federal jurisdiction.
The minister said that 90 per cent of negotiations are settled through the collective bargaining process in the federal jurisdiction. I think both sides can be justly proud of that. Among the 10 per cent that do not settle, that come to this forum, there are those who arrive here regularly before this House for legislated solutions because the system fails them.
I am not going to attack the employers in the grain industry here, because I think they, too, are caught with bad grain policies. But I am going to say to them that their need to provide a 12-hour day, 48-hour work week, to provide security for continuous operation, is an understandable one. However, I am also wondering why we are talking 12 hours a day, 48 hours a week.
I am pleased that the minister has assured us that he will not accept an arbitrated award because of the Canada Labour Code restrictions, and that both parties will have to negotiate that.
Recently a number of unions have negotiated 12-hour days and, because they freely negotiated it, that is fine if it is right for them. But, in fact, it is only now that the long-term effects of 12-hour days are being rediscovered. Fatigue, illness, stress, sleep disorders, digestive problems and workplace accidents. It is no accident that the mood in the workplace over the last 40 years has been to shorter, not longer hours. Why was it so important for us to hear the minister say that he is in favour, if proposed by the arbitrator, of an industrial inquiry commission into health and safety for the family life of this worker. It was important because we cannot afford unsafe work places, sick workers. We cannot afford that in this industrial society.
I know, just as the minister and the hon. member from the Liberal Party have said, that there is a tremendous cost to this dispute. But I also know that they used to ship through the port of Vancouver, 5 million tonnes a year, with thousands of workers. Today, they ship 17 million with 750 people. In fact, the union believes that it is possible to ship 20 million tonnes with the introduction of proper technological change.
What we need is good will. What we need is some
Government Orders
understanding that there is a long-term relationship between the settlements of the teamsters and the settlements of the grain workers. In fact, the grain workers had a three-year agreement with zero per cent in 1987, 2.1 per cent in 1988, and 2.8 per cent in 1989. The longshoremen at the same time got 7, 7, and 7. In this round of negotiations the employer has offered 4 per cent, when the longshoremen are already about 18 per cent ahead.
The same is true in Prince Rupert. The negotiations are not going well in Prince Rupert. For the government to undertake a pre-emptive strike before a dispute has taken place and to put legislation in place is merely the thin edge of the wedge. Maybe the minister is working toward having legislation in place: we can pass it all and the minute there is a dispute we can just impose it, we can proclaim it. That does not provide for free collective bargaining. We oppose the pre-emptive strike at Prince Rupert, Part II of the legislation.
In closing, I would like to say clearly that we are as opposed to legislating employers back to work as we are to legislating workers back to work. We are opposed to pre-emptive legislation, as shown in Part II of this legislation. We expect the minister to encourage the independent inquiry to look into the health and safety of family life of the worker it is facing in this legislation.
All the statistics in the world, all the legislation in the world, will not make a work place flourish. Only good will at both sides of the bargaining table will make that happen.

This is a piece of legislation which this government should have no pride in. This is a piece of legislation that should send shock waves across the country in the way it has handled itself with respect to this legislation. This is a very important bill for the maritimes. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission came to this government and said: "You are wasting money. You should be doing this in a different fashion. We can show you how to cut this program by up to 60 per cent and still provide that program to the maritimes". The government ignored it. Finally in 1989 when it did bring it in during the budget, there was actually no recognition of the work done by these good folks in the maritimes. When the matter was raised in the House and raised in committee, it had no idea that these studies had taken place.
This program was announced with obviously very little consideration, if any, to the various effects it was going to have on the region.
I know that the member from Halifax is upset with a few facts. She has a very good voice. If she wants to speak, I am sure she will have a chance later.
This has had a tremendous impact on the port of Halifax and on the port of Saint John. Enumerated many times by members of this party have been the cost in jobs, the cost in dollars and the potential future impact on that region of the country from the long-term closure of the grain elevators in Halifax and Saint John. It will potentially have a devastating effect on the livestock industry and on the dock workers in the maritimes. This is a bill with many tentacles. The loss of that program is going to wreak some real destruction in that region of the country unless there are some alternatives put in place.
When you look at western Canada, in my home province of Saskatchewan and throughout the west, it causes a lot of concern as well. We have in this country today a very great problem with the marketing of grain. There is a whole host of issues, a lot of it dealing with the European and the American trade war which has been going on for a while.

One of the important factors that has allowed us to maintain our market share is the Canadian Wheat Board. It has been working very hard to maintain the market share for western grain producers.
As the Canadian Wheat Board said when it was in front of our committee, the loss at the ports of Halifax and Saint John hurt the export grain industry. It hurt Canada's chances for grain export because those are the only two ice-free ports in Atlantic Canada.
As the Canadian Wheat Board told the legislative committee, all things being equal, a country with warm water ports would very likely not want to go to Montreal because it would have to deal with the ice in the wintertime and it may well cause the Canadian Wheat Board to lose sales.
The Canadian Wheat Board is doing what it can to ship grain to the Halifax elevator each year. It cannot afford to ship grain by rail during the wintertime and in the long run this could cost and will cost sales.
The other aspect is the long-term future of the Halifax elevator itself. Unless there is more grain going through that elevator, it will be closed. It was only through embarrassment of the government that it decided to call for a study on the future of the grain elevators in Atlantic Canada.
Saint John has already closed, and the study concluded that the long-term viability of Halifax, unless there is more revenue through that facility, will be threatened and it will ultimately be closed. That would simply be a tragedy not only to Atlantic Canada but to all Canadians.
It has been very frustrating dealing with this bill and it is not because there were no alternatives. There was a very viable alternative. There were some very serious issues. These were raised in the House and they were raised in committee, but the government chose to ignore them. It has ignored them at the peril of Canadians.
What it says to me and to many Canadians is that this government really does not give a damn for most regions of this country. It is a callous, mean-spirited government which is going to put through whatever it wants, period. It is a government with a second majority mandate mentality which is not good for Canada. It is not good for the regions of this country.
I would think that a good government is one that takes into account all relevant factors and then takes the course that will benefit the most people while inflicting the least harm on others. This is something that this government simply fails to do time and time again.
Government Orders
There is a real concern about unity in this country today. The Constitution is an extremely important document and issue. It is something that demands our attention, but there are some other areas in national unity that are also important. I would suggest to many Canadians, just as important.
This government, in many ways, has done as much to destroy national unity as it has ever done to promote it. There are concerns with communication and transportation, but there is a lack of concern for the regions of this country.
There was a time when Parliament concerned itself with the regions of this country. In many respects the national dream of John A. Macdonald was a regional development policy which encouraged the growth of western Canada.
It is only when governments stop paying attention to the regions of this country that this country is in real trouble. People in the maritimes are asking me: "What have you done to this area of the country?" Through the loss of the At and East, there has been a lot of movement of grain on the CN line to Halifax. VIA Rail has been cut. That cost money.
With the free trade agreement in place now, the CPR which has now purchased track all way through the United States to the eastern seaboard is promoting movement of goods from Montreal to New York. It is half the distance from Montreal to New York than from Montreal to Halifax. If that line loses any more goods being hauled on it, it will be the subject of an application for an abandonment by CN rail.
What we have is a situation in which this free trade agreement, this so-called right wing mentality, is destroying national unity and many maritimers are saying: "Why should I be part of Canada when I am paying huge taxes, GST, et cetera. I could buy my grain from Europe for $60 a tonne. I could haul com in from the U.S. and it would be better for us."
I see my time is up. I would like to take just a few more seconds to wind up by saying this. There is another debate coming up on the transportation of grain. It is coming up in western Canada with respect to the Western Grain Transportation Act. I really hope that this government pays a little more attention to that region of the country than it has to the maritimes. In committee, the member for Halifax told the government if that it is going to remove the At and East, it should remove the Crow benefit. That is the wrong attitude. I hope the member changes her mind.
