That, in the opinion of this House, the government should set specific markers to gauge the progress of the fight against child poverty in Canada so that it can be successfully eliminated by the year 2000.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take this opportunity to try to set the government's course for responding to the all party commitment that was made just a short time ago to end child poverty by the year 2000.
We all know that unless we set some agenda, some targets, some markers, it is very unlikely that we will know exactly where we are heading in the fight to eliminate child poverty.
I would like to take this opportunity to tell the House about Jessica, one of the 913,000 children in Canada living below the poverty line, one of the 560,000 who rely on food banks to provide their basic nutrition.
It is children like Jessica who form Canada's single largest group of poor people and the single largest group of food bank users. I will use Jessica as an example in order to put a face on poverty. This face is neither a "she" of statistics nor figures, which I will get into later, no, this face is of a four-year-old little girl, this face of poverty wears a small, sweet smile with baby teeth and big brown eyes looking to us for help. Jessica needs our help, as do the other 913,000 children living in poverty in Canada.
Her mother had to quit her $28,000-a-year job because she could not afford to pay $800 out of her $l,800-a-month pay cheque for child care. Her mother now receives welfare benefits to support the family but it is clearly not enough. Studies have shown that children from families who receive welfare benefits have one and a half times the rate of chronic health problems faced by other children, and 31 per cent of the children on welfare between the ages of six and 16 suffer from some psychiatric disorder. Children in the lowest income category are twice as likely to die before their 14th birthdays as children of wealthy families.

The problems do not stop there. Jessica will be four times as likely to do poorly in school, twice as likely to drop out before completing high school, and will have a high probability of underemployment or unemployment. She will also be more likely to turn to criminality or alcoholism when she grows up.
Surely, for none of us in Canada is this acceptable.
I am not only speaking about the plight of Jessica, but also the plight of one out of every six children in this country. We know the statistics and the consequences of these statistics, and we must do something other than lament about the problem in this House. This is a whole generation of children who need our help, and things are not getting any better. Current trends indicate that families' income status is deteriorating in Canada. Despite the government's enthusiasm for increased employment figures, the great majority of new jobs have been in the low-paying, part-time sector.
Let us look at what the government has done. The Prime Minister, as we all know, during the 1988 election campaign, said: "We will implement and build on our national child care program, the most innovative social advance in Canada since the Canada Pension Plan a quarter century ago".
Well, in November, 1989, the former leader of my party, Ed Broadbent, introduced a proposal to end child poverty by the year 2000, and the House unanimously adopted that motion. Following this with a speech to the United Nations Children's Summit last September, the Prime Minister spoke of the need for political will in meeting children's needs and challenged our children to listen carefully to what we say in the coming years to hold us to our commitments. And he said: "I hope we find that none of us will be wanting".
Actions taken by the government over the past year have not only not improved the situation, as promised, but in fact worsened it. We are now looking forward to challenge the Prime Minister and the government to own up to their promises and commitments and prove to Canada that these words were more than just a public relations ploy.
The children of this country need a lot more than just words to get them through each day.
Private Members' Business
The government established a children's bureau last year and the minister has been designated as the minister responsible for children, but we have not seen results from this bureau nor have we seen from it strategy to eliminate child poverty.
If such a plan exists, I hope we will see it, but we have no sign of that plan yet. I certainly hope that the bureau would not be advocating the policies of this government which are clearly throwing more children into poverty day by day.
In order to end child poverty by the year 2000 as the government has promised, as all the members on the government side and the opposition side have promised, something must be done now.
Just look at some of the facts. According to data recently released by Statistics Canada, the government's own statistical collection organization, in the first week of December 3.5 million Canadians or 13.6 per cent were living below the poverty line. There were 934,000, almost a million children under the age of 18, or 1 in 6 living below the poverty line.
Native babies in this country have about as much chance of living beyond their first birthdays as those in Jamaica and Costa Rica and at a higher risk than babies bom in Cuba and Singapore.
The same sorts of figures apply to poor, urban children in Canada too. In other words, our infant mortality rate does not compare very favourably with those of developing countries.
These figures clearly indicate a crisis situation. The only way to address the issue of child poverty is to examine the root causes of poverty.
The House subcommittee on poverty was told that children living in poverty are the sons and daughters of parents living in poverty, as one might expect. They were told that the economic status of children cannot be separated from the economic status of their parents. Any policy or program designed to eliminate child poverty, if it is to have a chance to succeed, must, of necessity, address the underlying reasons for poverty and its effects.

Private Members' Business
Far from doing this, through a series of legislative measures, the present Conservative government has made a lot of poor children poorer. To begin with, there is Bill C-69 which cuts funding, as we know, for health and post-secondary education in all provinces and caps the Canada Assistance Plan for British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
Over half of all welfare recipients, of all poor Canadians, live in these three provinces. Canada's child poverty rate does not fare well at all by international standards. Among industrial nations, only the United States has worse levels of family poverty than Canada. Our rates are three times those of Scandinavian countries for all families living in poverty and five times the rate for lone parent families.
Even Britain, having suffered under a decade of Thatcherism, has a poverty rate which is only half of that in Canada.
There has also been an attack on children by this government through inaction and omission. I am referring specifically to the lack of a national child care strategy. This must be a priority if we are to have any hope at all of ending child poverty in Canada by the year 2000 as the government has promised.
We have lived through decades under successive Liberal and Conservative governments who have followed policies which serve the corporate agenda rather than serve Canadians, especially those least affluent Canadians.
How much longer do we need to wait to see that these policies are not effective and are harmful to those who are most in need of help?
There are as many children living in poverty today as there were in 1980 and the acuteness of poverty felt by children and families is increasing. What is particularly alarming is the increase in the depth of poverty. The number of people who live at 50 per cent and 60 per cent of the poverty line has increased.
We are now faced with a recession. We have been in a recession and the number of children living in poverty is on the rise again. Over a decade of Liberal and Tory governments and there has been no real change to this situation.
Poverty can be defined as insufficient access to basic goods, services and opportunities which are commonly
available to non-poor Canadians and which are accepted as necessary to maintain a decent standard of living.
However, the implications of poverty go much further than this. Children growing up in poverty tend to have behavioural problems, low self-esteem, less motivation to learn, delayed cognitive development and lower achievement in school. They are at an increased rate of dropping out of high school and have a rate of poor health that is 150 per cent higher than the national average.
In December, 1990, the Canadian Association of Food Banks released preliminary figures from its 1990 hunger camp showing that half a million Canadians rely on food banks each month, a figure which is up 30 per cent from last year and between 40 and 50 per cent of the users are children. When asked what she wanted for her children, Jessica's mother said just that life be normal. Not that they have everything they want, but just what other kids have: warm clothes for the winter, good snow boots, nutritious food and a decent life. The sun and moon would be nice but let us be reasonable, just the basic necessities.
What Jessica's mother is asking for is not very much, I think, but it is more than she has now. In fact, the basic necessities are not things anyone should have to ask for. They should be taken for granted, especially in a country as wealthy as ours.
Article 27 of the recently adopted International Convention on the Rights of the Child states that every child has a right to a standard of living adequate for the child's physical, mental, spiritual and social development, and that it is a duty of countries within their means to see that this right is fulfilled, including the provision of material assistance and support programs particularly with regard to nutrition, clothing and housing.
Since the government has committed itself to ratifying the convention, I and Canada's children wait to see the actions and results. I ask the government to prove it is not just interested in talking about caring for children, but that it will also take an active role in caring for them. How else does the government propose to end child poverty by the year 2000? As we have seen it certainly is not going to go away on its own. Ignoring the problem will only make it worse.

Headstart type programs such as nutritional supplements for pregnant mothers and pre-schools for disadvantaged children are an approach apparently serving to lessen the burden on the poor in the United States. Better education, higher employment rates, and improved health are benefits of programs like this.
While this may be a quick fix for the program, longer term solutions are needed. Needs of children must come first on the political agenda. Problems like workplace, day care, flexible time, and extended parental leave are needed to assist parents when their children need not only material comfort but parental care also.
Children who are already living in poverty will need special assistance programs, not so much to give them a headstart but to let them catch up to their wealthier counterparts. A comprehensive strategy for addressing child poverty will require a concerted effort by government, industry and the Canadian public at large.
I would like to take this opportunity to make some suggestions to help eliminate child poverty by the year 2000. That is only eight and a half years away and there is a great deal left to do. There is no question that many working Canadians are now at a greater risk of poverty than ever. Although there are no quick fixes to the problems of the working poor, the major focus should be on education and job training.
Since the risk of poverty and unemployment is greater for those with less schooling this means a direct reversal of present government policy and it most definitely means the scrapping of Bill C-69 and Bill C-21.
Over the past few years there has been an erosion of support for families under the Conservative government. It has seen fit to take away from some the family allowance, a long-time accepted universal recognition of the importance of roles that parents play in our society.
We in the New Democratic Party believe that universal family allowance is a right that should not be taken away from parents. To take it away from so-called privileged families would be to turn it into another form of social assistance, something that would be available only to the downtrodden in society and yet another means of stigmatizing the poor. The family allowance has always been
Private Members' Business
accepted by Canadian taxpayers as a legitimate social program because everyone receives it, rich or poor. The moment this is taken away from some and given to a few is the moment that it is seen as a charity, not as a right.
In the short term the clawback of family allowance should be reversed and the allowance should remain fully indexed to inflation. There are advantages to this beyond just putting money in the hands of those who need it; family allowance payments provide a recognition of the important role of parents in our society in addition to putting money in the hands of consumers who will spend it and thus generate activity in the economy.
In the long term the government should focus its energies on a full employment policy. Those who would say that full employment policies have been attempted and have never worked are simply not aware of the facts. In truth, no Liberal or Conservative federal government today has paid anything more than lip service to the notion of full employment. Think about the philosophy of it; it clearly makes sense and it is clearly possible according to the most recent studies that I have read.
While it is true that many who are employed live in poverty is it still logical to assume that reducing the level of unemployment is a good strategy to reducing the level of poverty? The wage is the most stable source of income available to Canadians and providing all Canadians with a wage is the best way to ensure that all Canadians are provided for. Canada's economy must be made to work for Canadians. For governments such as this to consider 10 per cent unemployment normal while exporting jobs all around the world is remarkable and cruel. Full employment does not consider jobs created at minimum wage or part time to be particularly useful. Approximately half of Canadians living in poverty are employed and surely this would indicate some major problems.
Clearly if minimum wage jobs were to be offered as a viable employment alternative then the minimum wage must be raised substantially.
The concept of full employment does not end with providing jobs. It involves a commitment to providing sufficient social support systems to those who are unfortunate enough not to have jobs for a long or shorter period time.

June 14, 1991
Private Members' Business
A sustainable economy needs affordable, high quality, non-profit child care in sufficient numbers to meet the demands. It needs employment equity and decent wages, pensions and working conditions.
We should be instituting non-profit day care and universally accessible facilities and setting a time line for their installation. Full employment policy also requires a commitment to education, training and retraining.
Another tragic legacy of previous Liberal and Conservative governments is the rise of food banks in Canada. They started in the early eighties to help people through that recession. It has been almost a decade, and that recession has come and gone. We have had other recessions, and the demand for food banks is still rising.
Unfortunately, it is easy to see why food banks are needed. Social assistance rates across the country on average bring people up to half the poverty line. If a single mother is living in Prince Edward Island, she can receive 70 per cent of the poverty line on social assistance. But if she lives in Manitoba she will receive only 50 per cent of the poverty line.
The group of people in need of social assistance, thanks to the recession, high unemployment, aggressive changes to legislation, has grown. In Ontario, municipalities are finding welfare rolls are increasing at an alarming rate as more people move into the province hoping to find work.
A large number of children are included in these welfare figures, and as I said, children comprise the single largest group of welfare recipients across the country.
What is the government's response? The government says it is concerned about child poverty, and yet it chose to slap a limit on transfer payments to Ontario, Alberta and B.C. where half the poor in Canada live.
The government is probably hoping to pass the buck by expecting the provinces to pick up the pieces. Yet, these provinces are no better off financially than the federal government. They are finding it increasingly difficult to keep the social assistance system from collapsing. The end result is that children suffer and children remain in poverty.
How can this government say: "We are going to eliminate child poverty by the year 2000," when it is busy
putting even more people in the poorhouse. I am always happy to hear words of support for children, but in light of this present government's record, I say that children should not be holding their breath and waiting for action.
Instead of the backward steps that this government has taken, what are some of the forward steps we can take? How can we measure our progress? A number one priority as mentioned must be a full employment policy. Getting Canadians back to work is a sure way to see poverty among children decrease.
A national child care strategy with universal availability is needed. The development of low income housing must become a priority. Social assistance rates must be raised, and the government can encourage the provinces to do this by returning the 50-50 transfer payments to the provinces that the Canada Assistance Plan mandates.
The level of the federal minimum wage should increase substantially. Family benefits should return to full indexation and the clawback of family allowance must be revoked. The most obvious way to measure success in these areas is to monitor the number of children living in poverty.
Surely we can say that by the year 1995, which is half way to the end of the century, we should have reduced child poverty by half. We will not have achieved success if the numbers go down when the economy is good and up when it is not as has happened in the 1980s.
We should also set specific targets for percentages of needed child care spaces. By 1995, we might for example argue that half of these needs should be met. Similarly, availability of low income housing could be measured in the same way.
There is no question that any effective strategy to deal with child poverty will cost money. A government that has the courage and foresight to spend this money now as an investment in the future is a government that will receive the support of Canadian children and Canadian families.
Spending this money is critical as a necessary investment in Canada's future and will in the end provide Canada with a healthier economy and Canadians with a brighter future. The alternative is to live with child poverty and to sacrifice generations of Canadian children.

What I hope we can do in the context of this issue, one which has received non-partisan support across the House for all parties support eliminating child poverty by the year 2000, is to find some understanding of the need to set standards and targets so that we can eliminate child poverty by the year 2000.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for giving me the opportunity to speak today on the important social issue of poverty among children in Canada that was raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing.
His speech was very moving and there was a lot of well thought out information. I think all of us listened very carefully because we know that poverty and its effect on children and on families is a major concern for everyone.
For me, it is really a single issue which stands out as needing more time, more effort and more attention from all Canadians so we can put together a proper program. In fact, one of the major objectives of this government is to invest in our children and see them better educated, better protected and better nurtured so that they too can make their own contribution to our future here in this country.
In 1990 we watched children take on a new importance in world politics at the World Summit for Children, which was co-chaired by our Prime Minister. Leaders of 70 nations adopted the declaration on survival, protection and development of children and the action plan.
By signing this declaration Canada was urged to develop a plan of action and that is presently what we are doing.
Following this summit the Prime Minister asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare to undertake the task of presenting to the cabinet recommendations on these documents. One of the minister's priorities is to ensure better co-ordination and better consistency in areas addressing children's issues.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was just mentioning the establishment within the Department of National Health and Welfare of the children's bureau.
Since 1984 the federal government has embarked on a series of initiatives to improve the situation of Canadian families and protect the future of their children.
In the first instance, this government's approach has been to support self-sufficiency among Canadians through economic and social policies which have helped to create a climate in which job creation can prosper. In this regard, central to the recent federal budget is a plan for economic recovery that will put the recession behind us and will lead us forward to growth and prosperity.
This plan outlines strong actions and measures that will be taken to ensure fiscal responsibility in the government and legislated limits to government spending. We all know that the deficit and the debt are serious problems which must be solved. Each year we spend $1,650 for every Canadian man, woman and child on just servicing the debt.
We simply cannot go on living on borrowed money, money our children will have to repay.
Even in a time of necessary fiscal restraint, however, the government has acted to better support lower income families with children. This government has increased by more than 50 per cent the maximum value of the child tax credit since 1984 and has introduced a new child tax credit supplement for pre-school children. We have also eased the economic effect of marital breakdown on lone parents by offering services to help locate defaulting spouses and garnished federal moneys.
We have introduced the goods and services tax credit which ensures that families with incomes of less than $30,000 are better off after tax reform.
In addition, the federal government recently announced a four year, $136 million program to continue the effort at reducing the level of family violence in
Canada. The new initiative addresses violence against women, children, seniors and the disabled, and within the Indian and Inuit communities.
Social assistance and social services are matters of provincial jurisdiction. Provinces determine policies with respect to the services. Nonetheless the federal government does cost share in eligible provincial expenditures under the Canada Assistance Plan. Federal expenditures under the plan were about $6 billion in 1990-91.
Moreover, the federal government in co-operation with provincial governments is working to address the housing needs of disadvantaged Canadians. In 1990 through construction or renovation, over 42,000 new households were funded through federal social housing programs, and most of these programs were cost shared with the provinces andor the territories to address their shelter needs.
Over 640,000 households are now being assisted on an annual basis. Canadian children and their parents have also benefited from a series of new programs which will better prepare parents for participation in the labour force. These programs include employment ability in agreements with the provincial governments which help those people on social assistance with a transition from, say, welfare into the workforce; enhanced maternity and parental benefits to ease the transition back and forth from childbirth to the workplace for thousands of parents; and, the stay in school initiative which will combat the dropping out of school and will therefore better prepare the new labour force entrants for employment in the future.
As a result of these and other policies, there are some
956,000	fewer lower income people in Canada than there were when we took office in 1984, 300,000 of whom are children. Moreover, we are committed to a Canadian action plan for children which will address a broad range of issues which affect children, including child care.
We are also now actively working with the provinces toward the ratification, which is anticipated in 1991, of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. The convention is an important milestone in the expression of human rights for children. I can assure Canadians that a fundamental objective for this government is to protect the needy and enhance the well being of children in this country. This objective will be fully reflected in the plan of action in which we will spell out how Canada intends to implement the ten points of the world declaration signed by our Prime Minister at the World Summit for Children last September.

We are committed to prepare this plan by the end of
1991.	We are looking ahead to the end of the century and that is what our plan will involve.
We all have to recognize our duty to find innovative and effective solutions to break the devastating cycle of poverty.
,
I believe Canadians also recognize that the federal government alone cannot solve this problem. We cannot solve all the problems facing Canadian families and their children. We need teamwork between the Canadian families and the federal and provincial governments. We need the private sector and we need voluntary agencies. We all must work together. We will continue to do this to improve the well being of all Canadians.
In summary, I have to say to my colleague from the NDP Party that he has raised some very interesting and well constructed points. He said there is a need to set goals and targets, which is true. I look forward to the plan which will be put to the House at the end of 1991. We have taken steps to improve the economic well being of children and their families and the government is committed to continue its effort in this direction.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on behalf of my party on this very important subject of child poverty. I want to begin by complimenting the member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing for having introduced this motion and for his very well crafted and sincere words on a very, very important and disturbing subject for all Canadians; child poverty. I also want to commend him for the way in which he has crafted his motion, which speaks to the solution of the child poverty problem as opposed to simply describing the problem in more detail without having a thought of a forward plan.
The magnitude of child poverty in Canada is devastating and it ought to be at the top of the public policy priority list for all governments, in particular for the federal government, given the size of the problem. I just want to recite a few more statistics to give the House an
Private Members' Business
idea of what the magnitude of the problem is. 3.5 million Canadians are living below the poverty line, 1 million of whom are children. That is a ten-fold increase of children living in poverty since 1980 and a higher proportion of Canadian children living in poverty than in four other western nations, including the United States. Canada has the second highest rate of children living in severe poverty, which is defined as a family whose income is 75 per cent of the poverty line. Sixty-four per cent of poor Canadian children are rated as severely poor, with only the U.S. scoring higher at 57 per cent.
Clearly, these are devastating and stark statistics in a country which is as prosperous and as wealthy and has the abundance of natural resources that Canada has at the end of the 20th century. It clearly must be intolerable for us as Canadians to endure and to continue to accept this reality facing so many of our children, particularly in view of the fact that so many other things are correlated with child poverty: crime; the fact that poor children become poor adults; illiteracy; and the fact that so many of our poor children are native children. The consequences of poverty on our reserves are a national disaster and a national affliction.
One would have thought that the elimination of child poverty would be at the top of the government's priority list. I was looking for some statement to that effect and for some indication in the Speech from the Throne that the government was actually committed to a plan to eradicate child poverty by the end of the decade, particularly given the fact that the government has started to become specific with indicating performance targets and measures of performance for other aspects of its policies.
For example, in the last budget it was quite specific about its plan to reduce and eliminate federal deficits. Notwithstanding the fact that the plans of the previous finance minister, over the last seven years, have been completely and utterly off the mark the government did, in its last budget, produce very detailed, short and mid-term plans for reducing and eliminating the deficit. It apparently is soon to come forward with legislation which will set spending limits for itself.


Private Members' Business
In addition, it has talked about job creation by the end of the century. It has put a target on job creation and a target on education and the attainment of certain specific goals relating to illiteracy, to the number of Canadians with high school diplomas, and the number of Canadians with post-graduate degrees in mathematics, sciences and engineering. These goals are to make Canada more competitive internationally. We cannot fault the government for setting those kinds of targets. We may want to dispute the nature of the targets, but clearly that is something that should be in the Speech from the Throne.
Unfortunately, although the Prime Minister chaired the children's summit in New York last summer and the government had made specific commitments as a result of that summit, there is very little in the Speech from the Throne committing the government to really tackle the problem of eliminating child poverty in a very concrete way.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the hon. member was unable to finish his speech, but I also have some very important things to say, because eliminating child poverty by the year 2000 is very important, and I am sure we would all like to see that happen.
A country's children are the foundation and the future of that country. That is why during the past 150 years, governments throughout the world have taken steps to provide support for families and their children. The most recent manifestation of this philosophy was the Convention on the Rights of the Child, established by the United Nations. Canada has taken a systematic approach to family support. One of the key elements of the Canadian support system is the sharing of responsibilities by the federal govemement and the provincial governments.
x - i

Constitutionally, the provinces are responsible for ensuring the well-being of children through their social services and welfare programs. The federal government helps the provinces in this area by transferring funds through the Canada Assistance Plan and Established Programs Financing, for instance.
The federal concept of family benefits for children goes back to 1918, when amendments to the War Income Tax Act introduced the tax exemption for children. Later, in 1945, the family allowance program came into effect, thus proving that Canada recognized its obligation to educate its children. This program was intended as a mechanism for the government to supplement family income by relieving families of part of their expenses for the care and education of their children.
Since the introduction of family allowance, a number of changes have been made to adjust them to the requirements of families in need. Today, the federal government pays nearly $2.8 billion in family allowance to more than 3,500,000 families, for 6,500,000 children. The benefits are paid every month, usually to the mother, In 1991, the monthly benefit was about $34 per child.
Federal support for families goes beyond family allowance, however. There are a number of benefits for children, most of them provided in the form of tax credits. The Child Tax Credit Program aimed at low-income families is another major source of support for these families.
Since it came to power in 1984, the government substantially raised the ceiling of the credit by increasing it by more than 50 per cent-more remains to be done, but this is at least a good start-so that the actual benefit rose from $367 per child in 1984 to $585 in 1991. In 1988, the federal government introduced a supplement to the child tax credit for children up to six years of age. The supplement is $207 per child.
The government has also taken other steps to support the incomes of families with children. For instance, the implementation of a series of measures concerning goods and services will on the whole improve the financial situation of families with incomes below $30,000. These measures include an improved tax credit which is paid quarterly. The maximum value of the credit is $190 per adult and $100 per child.
Private Members' Business
We are also helping parents to use types of non-parental care that are not too costly. When they file their income tax returns, families can deduct up to $4,000 for child care expenses-work-related, of course-for children of pre-school age and up to $2,000 for children who are going to school.
Mr. Speaker, under the Canada Assistance Plan, which provides for cost-sharing with the provinces, the federal government helps fund eligible provincial expenditures for welfare and social services. In 1991-92, these expenditures will total $6.3 billion. Through this program, the government estimates it will pay about $250 million for child care.
The federal government intends to increase its support for child care through its National Strategy, which will deal with a number of issues that have an impact on children.
Families with new born infants will receive additional support, following amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. These amendments provide for a system of maternity, parental and health benefits. More specifically, fifteen weeks of maternity benefits during the period before and after the birth of the child; 10 weeks of parental benefits for natural or adopting parents-this is a new measure introduced by our government-for either the mother or the father; and 15 weeks of health benefits.
Under the new unemployment insurance system, the claimant will be able to receive benefits-up to the maximum amount for each type of benefit-as long as the cumulative period of special benefits does not exceed 30 weeks.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of outside pressures or constraints, a family may cease to function normally.
Since families are the basic unit of Canadian society, the federal government is concerned about these problems and wants to find ways to help families keep functioning effectively. It also knows that the public sector is in a position to provide substantial help, either directly or indirectly, to families experiencing a crisis. A number of federal initiatives designed to provide this type of support were launched recently.

Government Orders
One of our priority concerns is the issue of child sexual abuse and family violence in general, and we are tiying to provide assistance in this area.
Mr. Speaker, it is incredible that a society as advanced as ours, a society that is pluralistic and democratic, still tolerates violence against women and children. Yesterday we saw on television how a man who was obviously very distressed was holding his ex-spouse hostage. The same man had kidnapped his young child a few weeks before. It was done in desperation, I agree, but it is intolerable just the same.
Mr. Speaker, why, despite the measures I just mentioned, are there still so many poor families who are unable to get out of the poverty cycle? How can their needs be met? Should there be a guaranteed minimum income? Someone in my riding told me the other day that if instead of giving them a tax credit or a cheque in the mail, we gave parents food stamps, maybe then children would no longer go to school hungry.
Mr. Speaker, there is so much more to say, but I agree with hon. members that child poverty and child sexual abuse must stop now.
